items.text:
Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
- Published
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was the election's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually, external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.
In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis, Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".
Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.
The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."

What you need to know
- Ukraine's main European allies are convening in Berlin for 'Coalition of the Willing' talks
- Leaders of Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy are meeting at a time when President Donald Trump is set for talks with Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in China
- US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are also set to attend the meeting and will brief allies about discussions in China
Follow the latest on Thursday, 19th November, below:
'Coalition of the Willing' grouping is meeting in Berlin on Thursday
Germany's capital will host a meeting between a group of European leaders that support Ukrainein the war against Russia.
The meeting, dubbed the "Coalition of the Willing," includes German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will also be in attendance.
According to German officials, the meeting is intended to demonstrate the countries' commitment to legally binding security guarantees should a ceasefire agreement be reached between Russia and Ukraine.
The timing of the meeting is intended to allow the group to react quickly to announcements that come out of the meeting between US President Donald Trump ,Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping in China.
Trump might also meet Putin for a bilateral summit.
Welcome to our coverage
We'll be following updates from the so-called "Coalition of the Willing" meeting in Berlin.
The coalition is a grouping of countries that provide support to Ukraineagainst Russian aggression.
Leaders of Germany, France, Britain, Poland and Italy, as well as NATO head Mark Rutte, will attend the meeting today.
The show of support comes as Europe tries to forge a unified front in its attempt to be included in the US-led talks to end the war.
We'll have more from Germany's capital, thank you for joining.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, is set to rule in a landmark case accusing Myanmar of commit
items.text:
ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
The Gambia accused Myanmar of genocide following a 2017 military crackdown displacing over 730,000 Rohingya.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, is set to rule in a landmark case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority.
The reading of the judgment will begin at 10am (09:00 GMT) on Thursday at the Peace Palace in The Hague and is expected to last up to 90 minutes.
It could be the first time the court rules that a state has committed genocide.
The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has very limited means of enforcing it. If Myanmar ignores it, The Gambia could ask the UN Security Council to act.
What is the case?
The Gambia, a Muslim-majority West African country, brought the case in November 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
It argues that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide resulting from a 2017 military offensive that drove at least 730,000 Rohingya, who are mostly Muslim, from Buddhist-majority Myanmar into Bangladesh.
Survivors have recounted killings, mass rape and the burning of villages. A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the campaign included “genocidal acts”.
Myanmar denies genocide and says its forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups. It argues there is no direct evidence of an intent to destroy the Rohingya.
Why is it significant?
Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires proof of the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
The ICJ has never held a state responsible for committing genocide. In 2007, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, but ruled that Serbia had not itself committed genocide.
The judgment could also set precedents for other cases, including South Africa’s case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
The ICJ settles disputes between states, so it can find Myanmar responsible but cannot try individuals, which is the duty of the International Criminal Court.
The Gambia has asked the ICJ to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible, make reparations and ensure the Rohingya can return safely. Myanmar disputes The Gambia’s right to seek reparations on their behalf.
About 1.2 million Rohingya live in the Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement in Bangladesh, where many will follow the judgment, the Reuters news agency reported. Roughly 550,000 remain in Myanmar, with restrictions on their movement, healthcare and livelihoods.

A "sma
items.text:
COP31: Vanuatu calls for UN climate summit reform, warns of backsliding
Vanuatu's Environment Minister Ralph Regenvanu has called for changes to the UN climate summit process, accusing a small group of countries of blocking progress and warning that COP31 risks reversing previous commitments.
A "small group of states" is blocking progress at UN climate summits, as in other negotiations, Vanuatu's Environment Minister Ralph Regenvanu told AFP in an interview on Wednesday.
"There should be a reform of the COP process. We need to stop having this small group of states block progress and ambition for the rest of us", he said at the COP31 summit in Turkey, entering its last days.
The talks operate by consensus, but some countries, such as Panama, are pushing for majority voting to get around deadlocks.
Regenvanu leads his country's negotiations on climate issues, but also over a plastics treaty and at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), where Vanuatu last year secured an advisory opinion on climate.
Blocking was also happening "across all multilateral processes", he said, citing the plastics treaty as an example.
Negotiations to reach a treaty against plastic pollution began in 2022 under the aegis of the UN, but so far they have failed to make progress.
Read moreCOP31 deal draft foreshadows difficult route to consensus
Main blockers
Unlike many political leaders at the COP preferring to speak in general terms, Regenvanu named names.
"The Arab bloc and the LMDCs" are the main blockers, he said, referring to a bloc of around twenty developing countries that includes Saudi Arabia and India.
"Plus of course Russia."
Multilateralism was under threat all over the world, he said, "in no small part due to (US President Donald) Trump".
Climate negotiations in recent years have been hit by Trump's withdrawal of the United States, once again absent from the COP this year.
Also affecting discussions in Antalya are multiple geopolitical tensions between countries.
"We come here with high ambitions, but we have realistic expectations. We know it's a very difficult space."
Read more'Climate action is alive': Triumphant Democrats attend COP31 summit shunned by Trump
Risk of backsliding
The gap between developed and developing countries on the issue of finance is "deep and almost unbridgeable," he acknowledged.
"But our role as some of the most vulnerable countries is to try as much as possible to build bridges."
Vanuatu is part of the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), which in the past has often been among the most ambitious in climate negotiations, sometimes threatening to walk out in the absence of progress.
Its members, in the Pacific as well as in the Caribbean, are on the front line of climate change, facing rising sea levels and intensifying storms.
"There's a great risk of going backwards with this COP", Regenvanu said.
"Things we thought couldn't be threatened, that were agreed, are suddenly on the table. It's disappointing, but that's the reality we're faced with here."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.title: Xi-Trump-Putin talks live: China, US and Russia leaders to hold landmark three-way meeting
items.summary: The leaders of China, the US and Russia are set to hold a first-of-its-kind trilateral meeting on Thursday in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an APEC summit. The meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which Beijing said would involve "safeguarding world peace"
items.text:
The leaders of China, the US and Russia are set to hold a first-of-its-kind trilateral meeting on Thursday in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an APEC summit. The meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which Beijing said would involve "safeguarding world peace", has raised fears of a carve-up of the globe into "spheres of influence". Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will meet Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen for talks that have echoes of the US-UK-USSR February 1945 "Big Three" summit in Yalta.
The unprecedented trilateral summit of the leaders of China, Russia and the US will provide startling images and unsettle Europe this week, but all three presidents are approaching the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Trump says he looks forward to meeting with Presidents Xi and Putin
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he looked forward to his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Speaking at the start of the APEC summit in China's Shenzhen, Trump also said that his country has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years, and would continue to work to promote growth and stability, sovereignty, prosperity, and peace throughout the region.
Trump says historic summit with Xi, Putin already a 'win' before event
US President Donald Trump said his meeting on Thursday with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin was already a "win" before it took place, as China gave him a warm welcome.
The unprecedented diplomatic gathering of the leaders of the world's largest nuclear powers is unlikely to produce major agreements, analysts say, while it unnerves smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded.
In an interview with Fox News, Trump boasted about the pomp surrounding his arrival, which contrasted with the more muted greeting of other leaders, including Putin.
Global inflation calls for monetary policy tightening in many economies, IMF head says
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Thursday that energy supply shocks and Artificial Intelligence demand were accelerating global inflation to 4.7%, calling for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies.
Georgieva was speaking at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.
China's Xi calls for commitment to openness
Building an Asia-Pacific community requires a commitment to openness and integration, Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Thursday, calling for open cooperation as "essential toward the development and revitalization of the Asia-Pacific".
Xi was speaking at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.
Japan PM Takaichi spoke with Putin at APEC summit
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of a regional summit in Shenzhen, a foreign ministry official said Thursday.
The meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, Takaichi's first face-to-face talks with Putin since she took office last year, comes as relations between Tokyo and Moscow have soured.
The Japanese premier "conveyed Japan's positions" on issues including the ongoing detention in Russia of a Japanese journalist arrested on spying allegations and the recent seizure of Japan Tobacco assets, local media including public broadcaster NHK said.
The leaders "exchanged opinions" for around 30 minutes and agreed to maintain communication at various levels, reports said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, US leader Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin posed for a group photo at a regional forum on Thursday, ahead of a keenly watched trilateral summit.
Xi, Trump and Putin stood at the centre of the shot to mark the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, as other leaders, including Canada's Mark Carney, Australia's Anthony Albanese and Japan's Sanae Takaichi also took part.
Trump says Jensen Huang referred to 'just briefly' in his talk with Xi
US President Donald Trump said he spoke to Chinese President Xi Jinping about artificial intelligence but reference to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang only came up "briefly" in the discussion.
"We did not discuss it. I might have referred to it just briefly because it's such a tragedy. It's a tragedy. He's such a brilliant man," Trump said in an interview to Fox News that was broadcast during the network's "The Ingraham Angle" show.
What's on the agenda?
The agenda for the talks between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin remains unclear.
It is expected to include discussions of the Iran war and nuclear disarmament, according to Washington, after a US-Russia bilateral treaty on atomic weapons expired in February.
US officials had signalled that the Ukraine war -- something Xi vehemently sees as not China's problem -- was not expected to be addressed, before Trump said that it would.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga, speaking to reporters in Kyiv, said he hoped Xi and Trump would put "pressure on Russia to end the war".
But on the eve of the talks, Putin struck a defiant tone, saying Western sanctions provoked by the 2022 invasion had "failed".
Trilateral meeting to last under 60 minutes, Kremlin says
The meeting between the leaders of China, the United States and Russia is set to last less than 60 minutes, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has told Russian state media.
"No more than an hour" has been set aside for the historic summit, Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agencies.
Xi, Trump and Putin exchange greetings before historic meeting
The leaders of China, the United States and Russia exchanged greetings as they met in Shenzhen on Wednesday, a day before their history-making first formal trilateral summit in the Chinese city.

items.title: Why a trio of experts alleges Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide
items.summary:
Why a trio of experts alleges Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide
A new report alleges that injuries on Epstein’s body were overlooked by medical examiners during his 2019 autopsy.
A trio of experts has released a report casting doubt on whether convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein died by suic
items.text:
Why a trio of experts alleges Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide
A new report alleges that injuries on Epstein’s body were overlooked by medical examiners during his 2019 autopsy.
A trio of experts has released a report casting doubt on whether convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide in his jail cell in 2019, as a medical examiner in the United States previously ruled.
In documents obtained by Al Jazeera and other media outlets, Michael Freeman, Anders Eriksson and Itiel Dror – a forensic scientist, a forensic pathologist and a cognitive scientist – said the injuries on Epstein’s body were “most consistent with homicidal strangulation”, not suicide.
“The pattern, distribution, and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging,” their report reads.
Instead, they suggest Epstein was first assaulted and then strangled, providing an alternative narrative to the medical examiner’s 2019 report.
The cause of Epstein’s death has long been a source of controversy and conspiracy theories.
A wealthy businessman, Epstein cultivated a range of high-profile relationships with leaders in politics, industry, academia and the arts. His network of contacts included US presidents Bill Clinton and Donald Trump.
Those connections have raised questions about whether there was a cover-up of Epstein’s crimes – or whether some of his associates knowingly turned a blind eye.
In 2008, Epstein pleaded guilty to the solicitation of a minor for sex as part of a plea deal that saw him serve 13 months behind bars. Later, in 2019, he was arrested on federal charges of sex trafficking, with prosecutors accusing him of having “sexually exploited and abused dozens of underage girls”.
He died in a New York City jail while awaiting trial.
A controversy over cause of death
Medical examiner Kristin Roman performed the autopsy on Epstein’s body. She and New York City’s Chief Medical Examiner Barbara Sampson ultimately ruled that the evidence pointed to a suicide by hanging.
Other experts have sided with their ruling, pointing out that, while the circumstances of Epstein’s death were unusual, they are not necessarily inconsistent with suicide.
But Epstein’s brother, Mark, has long doubted the medical examiner’s findings. He gave Freeman, an Oregon-based forensic scientist, access to the death records.
Freeman has consulted in trials where families have questioned the narratives put forward by law enforcement about how someone died, including in high-profile cases like the murder of George Floyd.
Eriksson, meanwhile, is a Sweden-based forensic pathologist who has researched issues like shaken baby syndrome, a controversial diagnosis used to prosecute some adults for abuse of young children.
He and Freeman worked alongside Dror, a cognitive scientist who studies biases in forensic science.
At the time of his death, Epstein was a well-known figure, and Dror said the investigators handling his case would have been subject to significant political pressure.
“It’s so obvious this played a critical role in the examination of the body,” Dror told Al Jazeera.
“There was at stake a lot of emotion, a lot of people involved, a lot of politics involved, so many factors. You can list them for an hour, and all of those interfered and biased and influenced what should be a scientific decision.”
Dror explained that he and his colleagues pored over photos and records related to Epstein’s death and concluded that the medical examiner had wrongly ruled it a suicide.
Points of concern raised
In their report, the trio noted a number of issues with the initial investigation.
The prison personnel who found Epstein’s body did not take any photos before moving it, for instance. Investigators also failed to identify the ligature, the object that was actually around Epstein’s neck, they said.
They allege that some avenues of investigation went unexplored. The prison guard who first came across Epstein’s body initially refused to be interviewed, according to the report, and the medical examiner who determined the case was a suicide was not allowed to visit the prison.
The report also disagrees with the medical examiner’s assessment of Epstein’s injuries.
Marks left by the ligature on Epstein’s neck, the researchers said, were not slanted in the way that would be expected if his body had been hanging from the bedpost in his cell.
They observed bruising on Epstein’s back, shoulder and neck that they said was not acknowledged in the medical examiner’s original statements.
Those injuries, their report said, are “most consistent with homicidal strangulation from behind, most likely using a narrow knotted fabric ligature”.
Freeman, Eriksson and Dror believe either that the prison guard who found Epstein was lying about finding his body hanging in the cell, or that the body was deliberately put into that position to make it seem like a suicide had taken place.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike
items.text:
Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russian official says
- Published
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting mainland Russia to occupied Crimea.
The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.
The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.
It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.
Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.
At least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on Odesa on Wednesday, according to the regional state administration. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".
President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge as an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Ukraine used drones and missiles against it on 17 November which brought down a key section of the road.
That section of the double-arched, 12-mile bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
In response, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
While Ukrainian forces have struggled to close the bridge for good, recent attempts have brought them closer to destroying the bridge's crucial road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line.
Russian forces have also targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in recent days.
Russian strikes hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges causing traffic closures, partial damage to the metro system and some power and water outages.

The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction reco
items.text:
Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
- Published
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).
The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.
The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.
Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.
"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
Four other owners then had the painting.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

items.title: German FA backs France’s Diallo for FIFA presidency
items.summary:
German FA backs France’s Diallo for FIFA presidency
Incumbent Gianni Infantino has ignored repeated calls to resign, citing overwhelming global support.
The German Football Association (DFB) has said it fully backs French football chief Philippe Diallo’s bid to take over as FIFA president, cementing
items.text:
German FA backs France’s Diallo for FIFA presidency
Incumbent Gianni Infantino has ignored repeated calls to resign, citing overwhelming global support.
The German Football Association (DFB) has said it fully backs French football chief Philippe Diallo’s bid to take over as FIFA president, cementing his support in Europe.
DFB President Bernd Neuendorf announced the endorsement on Wednesday, two days after Diallo, president of the French Football Federation (FFF), accepted UEFA’s support to run against incumbent Gianni Infantino in March. European football’s governing body is eager for change at the top of FIFA.
“Philippe Diallo stands for a responsible approach to football and is determined to tackle the challenges facing the game in the years ahead,” Neuendorf said.
“He has a wealth of experience in international football and is widely respected throughout the European game. His approach to the role and the values he stands for are markedly different from those of the current FIFA president.”
The Dutch football association has also backed Diallo, with many European governing bodies expected to follow suit.
Diallo said on Tuesday that he has the support of countries beyond Europe.
“To beat him [Infantino] you need 106 votes, which is a majority,” he said.
“It is now up to me and my team to go and convince those on other continents, but already since yesterday [Monday] I have received spontaneous signs of strong support which will be revealed in the coming days.”
Opposition to Infantino
Infantino, who has led world football’s governing body since 2016 and is seeking a fourth term, has faced widespread opposition since his July attempt to sell stakes in future World Cups to private investors.
Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of the uproar, but UEFA has since gone to a court in Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the FIFA president in Switzerland.
Diallo announced in September that the FFF was withdrawing its backing for Infantino in the election, following similar announcements from other European associations. At the time, he said that “the trust placed in the FIFA president has been betrayed”.
Despite repeated calls for his resignation, Infantino maintains he has overwhelming support from member associations worldwide.
“We want football to change for the better. We want a FIFA that serves the game and acts in the interests of all its member associations,” Neuendorf said.
In addition to Diallo, who has headed the FFF since January 2023, Infantino faces challenges from top Japanese football official Kozo Tashima and Ramon Vega, an ex-Switzerland player.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.

items.text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.
Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He’s not saying he’s replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He’s saying he’s reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI.
The buyout was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit.
“Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” he explained.
For some people, “that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?” he added, “but, I mean, it has to be done.”
He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. “They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product.”
He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. “That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs.”
But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn’t grow up as an AI-first company. “So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?” he said. “It’s going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, ‘Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.’”
When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, “We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don’t have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution.”
He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. “All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity.”
In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. Elsewhere.

items.text:
Somalia’s constitutional overhaul tests its fragile federal bargain
President Mohamud’s reforms promise stronger government, but regional resistance and violence threaten the fragile deal of 2012.
Mogadishu, Somalia – A day before Somalia’s Supreme Court was due to rule on whether President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud had lawfully extended his term by a year, he abruptly dismissed the chief justice presiding over the case.
On November 4, the presidency removed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, citing complaints about the administration of justice. Five judges proceeded with the case the following day, ruling that constitutional amendments extending presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years could not apply retrospectively to those already in office. Their mandates, the judges said, had expired.
The government rejected the ruling and immediately swore in a replacement chief justice, setting up a direct confrontation between the president and the country’s highest court over the end of his mandate and the timing of elections.
The standoff marks the latest escalation in a two-year political contest over Mohamud’s proposed constitutional changes.
Intended to address long-standing structural problems that have hindered Somalia’s reconstruction, the changes have instead deepened divisions over the country’s political future, the nature of its federal system and the distribution of power.
Mohamud and his allies believe stronger national institutions, clearer rules and direct elections will help advance Somalia’s decades-long state-building project.
The deadlock has increasingly spilled beyond parliament and political negotiations, with tensions playing out on the ground.
Two federal states have suspended cooperation with Mogadishu, while disputes elsewhere have turned violent. In June, clashes between government forces and militias guarding a former president and prime minister brought part of the capital to a standstill for two days.
A federal bargain left unfinished
Somalia’s effort to rebuild a functioning national government is one of the world’s longest-running state-building efforts, hampered by a decades-long civil war.
After the central government collapsed in 1991, regional administrations emerged around clan alliances, building their own institutions, security forces and revenue streams.
Somaliland was the first to emerge from the ashes of Somalia’s civil war, declaring independence in 1991. Puntland followed in 1998, establishing an autonomous administration. Other regional administrations emerged in subsequent years, eventually forming part of the country’s evolving federal system.
The provisional constitution adopted in 2012 established a federal framework for sharing power between Mogadishu and the regions. However, some of the most contentious questions over the division of powers and control of resources were deferred as national institutions took shape.
Those unresolved questions made governance dependent on constant negotiation. Elections depended on agreements among regional leaders and clan elders, while disputes over power and revenue repeatedly delayed national decisions in the absence of consensus.
“Control of ports and trade routes, and relationships with foreign governments, gave some considerable independence from Mogadishu,” Jethro Norman, a Somalia expert at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told Al Jazeera.
Norman said Mohamud’s overhaul seeks to give Mogadishu greater legal authority over areas that regional administrations have long controlled, although enforcing that authority is another matter.
“What you’re seeing is the federal system crystallising into two camps,” he told Al Jazeera. “You have Villa Somalia presenting the constitution as completing the state: one person, one vote, multi-party politics, democracy, central federal control over foreign relations and national security, and so on.”
Puntland and Jubaland, by contrast, see the changes as an imposition that undermines the original federal bargain.
“Their view is that the 2012 constitution was a bargain between the centre and the regions, and it can’t just be re-written through a parliamentary majority in Mogadishu when the regions have rejected it,” Norman said.
Some federal states retain close commercial and security ties with the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which Mohamud, who has frosty ties with Abu Dhabi, has accused of supporting regional leaders in their disputes with Mogadishu.
In January, Mohamud’s government announced the cancellation of the UAE’s port and security agreements across Somalia. The regional states, however, rejected the decision.
The dispute has added to tensions over the future of the federation. Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni, whose administration is among Somalia’s most autonomous, has even suggested that the country may need to reconsider how it holds together.
“If a solution is not found for the current debate, Somalis must deliberate and decide on another alternative way to live together,” he warned.
The stakes have also grown with international recognition of Somaliland. Israel became the first United Nations member state to recognise the breakaway northern region at the end of 2025.
Somali academic Afyare Elmi told Al Jazeera that the government was weakening the fragile consensus underpinning the 2012 settlement by pushing through constitutional changes it could not enforce in states that opposed them.
“This is one of the most dangerous times the Somali political system has faced,” he said. “Somalis are no longer moving in the same direction on the future of the state.”
Completing the constitution
Mohamud himself helped shape the federal system he is now seeking to overhaul.

items.text:
Almost 1 in 4 children live in conflict zones — report
November 19, 2026
A record number of children were living in a conflict zone in 2025, Save the Children findings revealed on Thursday.
In the latest report in the "Stop the War on Children" series, the humantarian group said 589 million children worldwide lived in conflict zones. That's the highest number since records began in 1990, and more than double the total in the mid-1990s.
"For millions of children, fear, violence and displacement are part of every day life," said Save the Children Germany CEO Florian Westphal.
He said this needed to be a "wake-up call" for the international community.
Where children are living in conflict zones
Around two in five children in both Africa and the Middle East were living in conflict zones in 2025, the report found. Africa, alone, accounted for 44% of all children living in conflict zones worldwide.
In terms of regional proportions, 40.2% of children in the Middle East were living in conflict zones in 2025. That represented roughly two in five children across the region, and a particularly steep rise in the number of children affected. The figure jumped by nearly 29% from 52 million in 2024 to 67 million last year.
Children's exposure to conflict in Africa has more than tripled over the past 15 years, with the share of children living in conflict zones rising from 12% in 2010 to 39% in 2025.
Grave violations against children in armed conflict zones increase
The report highlighted the dramatic increase in the denial of humanitarian access.
A total of 8,322 verified incidents of denying access to humanitarian aid to children were recorded in 2025, a 16-fold rise over the past decade. The figure was 509 in 2015, and only eight incidents were reported when the United Nations (UN) established the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM) in 2005.
The Palestinian Territories accounted for the vast majority of cases, with 5,946 incidents, or more than 70% of all verified cases globally.
"No grave violation has increased as dramatically or changed the overall pattern of verified violations as much as the denial of humanitarian access," the study noted.
According to the report, denial of humanitarian access rose from around 2% of all verified grave violations against children in 2015 to more than 21% in 2025, becoming the second-most frequently recorded violation after the killing and maiming of children.
Grave violations as laid out in the MRM also include the recruitment of children by armed forces, sexual violence, abduction and attacks on schools and hospitals.
Where violations against children were concentrated
The study found that, overall, 38,967 grave violations against children were verified by the UN.
This was the second-highest annual total since the MRM was established, surpassed only by the record 41,763 violations documented in 2024.
More than half of these took place in just three areas: the Palestinian Territories, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria. The Palestinian Territories alone accounted for 12,449 verified violations, nearly one-third of all cases.
As well as the denial of humanitarian access, violations in 2025 included:
- 14,224 children killed or maimed in conflicts in 2025
- A record 5,128 child abductions
- 1,787 cases of sexual violence, a 71% increase in the past decade
- A fifth straight year of increased attacks on schools and hospitals, at 2,930 cases
The Palestinian Territories recorded the highest number of attacks on schools or hospitals, with 837 incidents, followed by Ukraine with 643. Together, the two accounted for more than half of all reported cases worldwide.
The sharpest rises in sexual violence incidents were recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where cases jumped from 358 in 2024 to 592 in 2025, and Sudan, which saw an increase from 74 to 193. Around 86% of all cases were documented in African conflict zones.
"Children have the right to live free from violence. Changing the odds requires political choices that put children’s safety first, and a sustained commitment to stop the war on children," the NGO said.

items.title: Ex-U.S. coach Arena: Federation 'don't have a clue' how to replace Poch
items.summary:
Former United States men's coach and current San Jose Earthquakes manager Bruce Arena called out U.S. Soccer as the federation searches for Mauricio Pochettino's replacement.
Pochettino was confirmed as Manchester United's new head coach on Nov. 13, leaving the USMNT after more than two years in cha
items.text:
Former United States men's coach and current San Jose Earthquakes manager Bruce Arena called out U.S. Soccer as the federation searches for Mauricio Pochettino's replacement.
Pochettino was confirmed as Manchester United's new head coach on Nov. 13, leaving the USMNT after more than two years in charge.
U.S. Soccer said the federation would begin the search for a new coach with U23 manager Steve Cherundolo overseeing a December camp and friendly against Jamaica next month.
"In my view, they don't have a clue what they are doing," Arena said on Wednesday when asked about the search.
Pochettino led the United States to a 2-0 victory over Haiti on Nov. 17 in his final game in charge before immediately departing for England. Combined with a 6-0 win against Haiti in the first leg, the U.S. advanced 8-0 on aggregate to the Concacaf Nations League finals.
This wasn't the first time that Arena, who served as USMNT coach from 1998 to 2006 and again from 2016 to 2017, was critical of the hiring of Pochettino. The San Jose Earthquakes manager said in 2025 that a non-American lacked the necessary understanding of the country's culture to manage the Americans.
"You know if you look at every national team in the world, the coach is usually a domestic coach," Arena said on the "Unfiltered Soccer" podcast with former USMNT stalwarts Landon Donovan and Tim Howard in 2025. "I think when you're a national team coach, you need to know your environment, you need to know the animals you coach, and we're lacking that. If you're an American coaching the U.S. team, you know the culture, you know the pride and how important the national team is. I think when you bring in somebody from the outside, they don't understand it, especially in our country, because we're so different."
Arena currently stands as the USMNT coach with most victories recorded in his tenure. During his first stint, Arena managed 71 wins, 30 losses and 29 draws, and led the Americans to the quarterfinals of the 2002 World Cup. He returned in 2016 and took that tally to 81 wins, but infamously fell short of guiding the team to qualification for the 2018 World Cup.
Arena is preparing the San Jose Earthquakes for its round one matchup with Houston Dynamo FC in round one of the 2026 MLS playoffs.
"We played Houston twice this year," Arena said on Wednesday. "They know us, we know them. So there'll be no surprises. It will be a battle, like any playoff series in any sport. It'll be strongly challenging. We're hopeful that the home field advantage means something."
San Jose hosts Houston in game one of the best-of-three series on Nov. 24.

Pochettino's final act in charge of the United States national side was a 2-0 victory over Haiti in Cincinnati on Tuesday night.
A plane carry
items.text:
Mauricio Pochettino arrived at Manchester United for his first day as head coach on Wednesday but said he requires "time" to turn the club's fortunes around.
Pochettino's final act in charge of the United States national side was a 2-0 victory over Haiti in Cincinnati on Tuesday night.
A plane carrying Pochettino arrived at Manchester Airport on Wednesday afternoon. He headed to the club's training ground, Carrington, as the replacement for the sacked Michael Carrick before his first game leading United on Sunday against Liverpool at Anfield in the Premier League.
On Tuesday night, Pochettino was told by former Manchester City and United States player DaMarcus Beasley that "Manchester is blue, it will always be blue."
He responded: "You will see. Give me time.
"The new challenge is a big challenge, but at the same time it's adrenalin you want to feel. We need to add our common sense... we know the situation is not a situation that deserves to be a club like Manchester United, the fan base is amazing."
Pochettino added: "The mentality is to learn from everyone. You need to have an open mind because I think the players can teach us every day, we are much better coaching staff now.
"Football is about attitude, and it's about the approach. It's about connection, feelings and communication."
Upon arrival at Carrington, Pochettino said he is "very excited to be here. It's an honour. It's a privilege to be in this amazing club. Yes, looking forward to start to work."
United have confirmed Jesus Perez, Miguel D'Agostino, Toni Jimenez, Alec Scott and Sebastiano Pochettino as Pochettino's staff.
Mauricio Pochettino starts work at Man United on Wednesday
Pochettino was also asked about whether he can improve United's running statistics, which were criticised by ex-boss Carrick after a drab 4-1 loss to Como in the Champions League.
In response to Bruno Fernandes' questioning of the team's tactics, Carrick said: "Whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you ain't going to win."
Pochettino said on Tuesday night: "What I can talk in general, football is very complex and I think it's not important if you run or not run.
"You need to run well, you need to run with an objective, you need to run together. Then you need to play, you need to know what you need to do, you need to express your talent. The mindsets are so important."
Pochettino led the U.S. to the round of 16 at last summer's World Cup on home soil.
But he is now returning to the Premier League where he has previously coached Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea.

items.title: USWNT's Emma Hayes on role in USMNT coach search: 'Through a technical lens'
items.summary:
United States women's national team coach Emma Hayes said that she's committed to helping with a thorough search for the next men's national team coach after the recent exit of Mauricio Pochettino.
On Tuesday, Pochettino managed his last game for the U.S. men, a 2-0 win over Haiti in the quarterfina
items.text:
United States women's national team coach Emma Hayes said that she's committed to helping with a thorough search for the next men's national team coach after the recent exit of Mauricio Pochettino.
On Tuesday, Pochettino managed his last game for the U.S. men, a 2-0 win over Haiti in the quarterfinals of the Concacaf Nations League, before departing to Manchester United.
"I'm very embedded into the federation, and I work really closely with [U.S. Soccer CEO] JT [Batson], in particular, and even more so with [U.S. Soccer COO] Dan [Helfrich] as we're growing to develop the American soccer movement and JT asked if I would be involved as a technical voice, to be involved with the process," Hayes said.
"I feel confident in the group of people that have been put together to create a thorough process to select the next men's national team coach, and my role is merely to support that through a technical lens, knowing I do this job at least, albeit with the women's team, and that I've coached for a number of years and can offer some of that insight into the application of what to look for and why."
The federation announced last week that Hayes would be part of a group that would look for the next men's coach.
"Batson and U.S. Soccer Chief Operating Officer Dan Helfrich, alongside the soccer leadership team at U.S. Soccer that includes Emma Hayes and Oguchi Onyewu, will lead the search for the next USMNT head coach, drawing on input from leaders across U.S. Soccer and the global soccer landscape," said U.S. Soccer. "The Federation will consider candidates from a broad range of backgrounds."
Hayes is currently preparing for a Concacaf W Championship quarterfinal against El Salvador on Nov. 27. The winner of the single-leg knockout match will qualify for the 2027 Women's World Cup.
Pochettino was asked on Tuesday if he'll be available to help the U.S. Soccer Federation pick his successor, but the Argentine said he wouldn't be participating in that process.
"I think it's not my job. And for sure they have the capacity and the knowledge to find the right people with the right profile," he said. "I don't know how to measure my colleagues and I think it's not my job.
"More than two years ago they signed Emma Hayes [for the U.S. women's national team] and then Mauricio Pochettino. I think they have good eyes. They have good taste of football."
Former U.S. international Steve Cherundolo will oversee the final USMNT game of the year against Jamaica on Dec. 13 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.
The U.S. will play its next competitive match in late March at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles against Mexico for the Nations League semifinals.

Midfielder Sam Coffey has been named to the United States women's national team's World Cup qualifying roster that will assemble for training camp later this month, marking her first time with the team since April.
Coffey, a starting midfielder for the U.S. during its 2024 Olympic gold medal run, ha
items.text:
Midfielder Sam Coffey has been named to the United States women's national team's World Cup qualifying roster that will assemble for training camp later this month, marking her first time with the team since April.
Coffey, a starting midfielder for the U.S. during its 2024 Olympic gold medal run, had a minor knee operation in the spring that kept her out of the past two international windows.
The U.S. will be without stalwart defender Naomi Girma again due to ongoing recovery from a series of calf injuries.
Girma also last played for the U.S. in a series of exhibitions against Japan in April.
On Wednesday, U.S. head coach Emma Hayes announced her 23-player roster for the World Cup qualifying event.
The U.S. will play El Salvador on Nov. 27 in the quarterfinals of the single-elimination Concacaf tournament in Mansfield, Texas.
All four quarterfinal winners automatically qualify for the 2027 Women's World Cup, while the losers go into a play-in bracket for a change to advance to the global playoff.
About Girma's injury, Hayes said she was working closely with Chelsea.
"I've been speaking with Naomi a lot in the last few weeks," Hayes said in Wednesday's news conference. "I think there's been a really good club and country collaboration to get it right, because it's critical, and it's critical for a career that no detail is too small to be able to do that. I think in an ideal world we wouldn't be in the position that we're in.
"But listen, the human body reacts and responds to different stimulus in different ways, and I think Naomi has certainly grown an appreciation for not just taking a key role in her rehab, but being really thoughtful around and intuitive about a body, in relation to that.
"But we want to be right. We want to get it right. It's not about being first. I don't think we can afford --- anyone --- Naomi, Chelsea, USA, we have to make sure we are incredibly thorough to ensure that Naomi gets back on the pitch as soon as possible."
Angel City FC defender Evelyn Shores returns to the roster after receiving her first senior call-up last month for games against Spain (she did not play in a game).
Shores is just the second uncapped player in USWNT history to be named to a World Cup qualifying roster.
NWSL Golden Boot winner Ashley Sanchez and fellow forward Mallory Swanson also return to the roster.
Both players made their returns to the field for the U.S. against Spain and scored in the U.S.' 2-2 draw with the world's top team on Oct. 13.
"It's been a great year of growth and learning for our team, and for a long time the focus has been on qualifying for the World Cup, so now that time has arrived," Hayes said in a statement.
"I want to see relentless consistency from our players, individually and as a team, and I want us to be elite in both penalty boxes. If we can achieve that, I'm confident those performances will carry us through to meet our standards and goals. This is my first Concacaf event and the first for many of our players, so we're all looking forward to the experience."
Only seven players on the roster have World Cup qualifying experience, with only three of them -- Swanson and midfielders Lindsey Heaps and Rose Lavelle -- playing in multiple qualifying tournaments.
"Qualifying for a major tournament, first and foremost, I'll be leaning on our experienced players," Hayes said. "They know how to do this, and they've been with us the longest to be able to deliver that, and I think [also] for the less experienced players who have had a good body of work in the last couple of years, so we know what we need to do.
"We need to just make sure we come into camp with really clear mind about those things. Focus on the only game in front of us."
Goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn also returns to the roster after her outstanding performance for the Utah Royals in the NWSL quarterfinals earlier this month.
Utah teammate and defender Kate Del Fava also returns after receiving her first call-up and first cap against Spain on Oct. 13.
Forwards Jaedyn Shaw and Ally Sentnor, who had been regular USWNT call-ups in recent years, are again absent from the senior roster.
Hayes reiterated that no player has a guaranteed roster spot for the World Cup next year.
"We don't want players that are in our group that are in a place where they're not fighting to improve every day or be as competitive as they could possibly be," she said.
"But I think when players have stacked and accumulated a lot of experience over a period of time, that is always going to put them in a steady position. But it doesn't guarantee anything.
"I will be unafraid to leave anybody off that plane if I don't feel that they are applying themselves to put ourselves in the best possible position to compete, which is why this upcoming camp, our job is to qualify for the World Cup, and so everything we have worked towards is ensuring that every player that comes into camp makes sure they lift their level."

items.title: Bay FC signs England defender Jess Carter from Gotham FC
items.summary:
Jess Carter is trading the east coast of the U.S. for the west after signing a deal with Bay FC, the NWSL side announced Wednesday.
The England international, who was part of the Lionesses' 2022 and '25 European Championships squad, spent the last three seasons playing for Gotham FC, winning multipl
items.text:
Jess Carter is trading the east coast of the U.S. for the west after signing a deal with Bay FC, the NWSL side announced Wednesday.
The England international, who was part of the Lionesses' 2022 and '25 European Championships squad, spent the last three seasons playing for Gotham FC, winning multiple trophies including the NWSL Championship in 2025.
Carter, who was a free agent, has a contract with Bay FC that runs through 2028 with an option for 2029, the club said in a release.
"Coming to Bay FC is a new challenge, and that's something I'm excited about," Carter said in the release. "I've been fortunate to be part of some successful teams, and I know how much work goes into winning. I'm looking forward to getting to know this group, earning the trust of my teammates and doing my part to help us move forward."
Carter, 29, was a fixture at the heart of Gotham's defense in 2026, playing all 30 games during the regular season and starting both matches in the NWSL playoffs. Defending champions Gotham were eliminated in the semifinal by the Kansas City Current.
"Jess has consistently demonstrated her quality in championship-winning environments at both club and international level," said Bay FC chief football officer Paul Green. "Having worked with her at Chelsea, I've seen her development and the professionalism she brings every day. She will bring valuable experience to Bay FC, and we're delighted to welcome her to the club."
Before joining Gotham in 2024, Carter was part of a Chelsea side that won five consecutive Women's Super League titles.
Carter has made 56 appearances for England and was on the 2023 World Cup team that lost to Spain in the final. She was recently picked in the squad that will face Ukraine in a December doubleheader that serves as a qualifier for the 2027 World Cup.
Information from ESPN Global Research was used in this report.

items.summary:
Manchester United are prepared to mount legal action if they find evidence that JJ Gabriel has been illegally approached by other clubs while under contract, sources have told ESPN.

items.text:
Manchester United are prepared to mount legal action if they find evidence that JJ Gabriel has been illegally approached by other clubs while under contract, sources have told ESPN.
Gabriel announced his departure from Old Trafford with a video posted on social media on Tuesday. Sources have told ESPN that United were unaware of the announcement until it was published.
United still hold Gabriel's registration and sources have told ESPN there has been no contact with any governing body about transferring the 16-year-old's registration to another club.
A verbal agreement is in place for Gabriel to sign for Real Madrid. He can join a club within the European Union as a domestic or EU player, bypassing non-EU foreign player quotas, because he has an EU passport.
Real Madrid were approached for comment by ESPN but have not yet responded.
The teenager has not been back to Carrington since walking out in September.
Sources have told ESPN that United staff have made a number of attempts to check on Gabriel's welfare, but have not been able to make contact with his family.
United, according to sources, believe Gabriel's family and representatives may have held meetings with rival clubs as early as last summer.
Gabriel refused a request from United to train with the academy at the start of preseason before joining the first-team squad on a full time basis. A number of demands were also made by his representatives ahead of the season.
They included Gabriel playing at least 20 minutes in first-team games against Sabah FK, Brighton and Bournemouth, for the forward to be assigned the No.77 squad number and to have the name "Gabriel JR" on his shirt.

items.text:
Anthropic raises $81.3bn in biggest IPO of all-time
AI giant prices shares at $83 in blockbuster market debut.
Anthropic has raised $81.3bn in the biggest initial public offering of all-time, leapfrogging SpaceX’s $75bn market debut in June.
The AI giant said in a statement late on Wednesday that the company and its seven co-founders had sold 980 million shares at $83 each.
The bigger-than-expected IPO comes after investor demand for the stock far outstripped anticipated demand.
Anthropic had said in corporate filings last week that it intended to offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 apiece.
The blockbuster offering puts Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former researchers of OpenAI, on track for a market value of roughly $1.5 trillion, which would make it the world’s 12th-biggest firm at current valuations, just behind Tesla.
Anthropic shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT.”
Anthropic’s market debut has been closely watched as a test of the eye-watering valuations of tech companies leading the rollout of AI.
Jay R Ritter, an expert in IPOs at the University of Florida, called Anthropic’s valuation unprecedented for such a young company.
“Investors are excited about its software, which may allow drug companies to find drugs capable of preventing cancer and dementia within ten years,” Ritter told Al Jazeera.
“Thirty years ago, the internet was the next big thing. It has changed our lives. Today, artificial intelligence is the next big thing,” Ritter said.
More to follow…

An unvaccinated resident of Pennsylvania has died after contracting measles, marking the eighth measles-rel
items.text:
Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies amid historic US measles resurgence
Pennsylvania records eighth measles death of 2026, a day after the US formally loses its 26-year elimination status.
An unvaccinated resident of Pennsylvania has died after contracting measles, marking the eighth measles-related fatality in the northeastern state this year.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed the death on Wednesday and said it had been reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
While the department did not publicly identify the individual who died, it said they were a resident of Clinton County, in the centre of the state.
The latest death comes shortly after the United States formally lost its measles elimination status, a designation it held for nearly 26 years.
That status indicated that measles was not endemic to the US, meaning no single strain had circulated continuously for 12 months or more.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a branch of the World Health Organization, updated the US’s designation on Tuesday after reviewing transmission data from the country.
The US is grappling with its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades. As of November 12, the CDC had counted 5,412 confirmed cases since the start of the year.
Pennsylvania, meanwhile, reported 1,589 cases across 46 of its 67 counties. The state’s health agency pledged to continue its aggressive response to the outbreak.
“Approximately 300 DOH staff are proactively working with residents, community organizations, and health care providers to combat the measles outbreak in the Commonwealth through access to fact-based information and access to the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine,” the department wrote in a news release.
The agency also said state health officials have administered more than 11,500 MMR vaccine doses in 2026, including more than 7,200 shots in pop-up clinics since the outbreak erupted in late April.
Experts say vaccine hesitancy in recent decades has contributed to the rising number of cases.
Measles is highly contagious and can spread quickly, particularly when someone coughs or sneezes. The virus can survive for up to two hours in the air, and an estimated 90 percent of those who are not immune will catch it upon exposure, according to medical authorities.
Critics point to leadership under US President Donald Trump as contributing to the measles outbreaks.
One of Trump’s cabinet officials, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, has questioned the efficacy and safety of vaccines like the MMR shot.
He also said in an interview with NewsNation that the MMR vaccine “contains a lot of aborted foetus debris and DNA particles”, an unsubstantiated claim.
Still, he encouraged vaccination in a social media post on Tuesday, following PAHO’s decision to revoke the US’s measles elimination status.
“We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” he wrote.
The CDC also said it remained committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Erica Schwartz said.
Before taking office in early 2025, Kennedy claimed that no vaccine was “safe and effective” and promoted the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism.

European Union governments have approved the signing of a previously agreed trade deal between the EU and Indo
items.text:
EU governments approve trade deal with Indonesia to offset Trump tariffs
The deal, initially concluded in 2025, will see both sides remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products.
European Union governments have approved the signing of a previously agreed trade deal between the EU and Indonesia aimed at offsetting the impact of United States President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
The Council of the European Union’s decision on Wednesday also allows the deal to be applied provisionally. Both sides will remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products, and Indonesia’s 50 percent duty on EU cars will be eliminated within five years.
The deal will tie one of the world’s top economic blocs more closely to the fourth most populous country.
“These agreements will make it easier for European businesses to trade and invest, remove tariffs on almost all goods traded between the EU and Indonesia, and save businesses an estimated €600 million [$658.3m] annually in customs duties,” said Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Helen McEntee.
Indonesia has been negotiating a free trade and investment agreement with the EU since 2016. However, relations became strained after the European Commission decided to phase out palm oil from transport fuel by 2030 and imposed anti-subsidy duties on Indonesia’s biodiesel exports.
Both sides want the agreement, initially concluded in September 2025, to be applied as swiftly as possible. Indonesia will graduate from the EU’s generalised scheme of preferences on January 1, 2027, after which its exports will no longer benefit from preferential tariffs, the Council said in a statement.
The EU and Indonesia will now sign the agreements, which will then be submitted to the European Parliament for approval.

items.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI released as gamers rejoice globally
November 19, 2026
Grand Theft Auto VI will be officially launched Thursday, ending a 13-year wait for one of the most anticipated games ever.
The game will become playable at midnight local time (CET) on a wide range of platforms, including PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, meaning gamers in Asia will get to play the game ahead of users in the US and Europe.
In New Zealand, one of the first countries worldwide where the game became available, the release prompted internet providers to prepare for a spike in internet usage at midnight.
This comes due to the game's size of 212 gigabytes, more than a quarter of the average New Zealand household's usage in a month.
Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA franchise, faces high expectation after 13 years of anticipation, with previous versions having become commercial and cultural hits around the world.
GTA games sold 470 million units worldwide, and the fifth installment generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days after its release in 2013.
GTA's global success
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar Games' parent company, saw its shares rise by more than eight percent the day before the game's release.
The game takes place in Vice City, a fictional version of Miami.
It follows Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple drawn into criminal networks while trying to secure a better life. GTA games are often criticized for including excessive violence and for glorifying crimes and drug use.
Lucia, a former prisoner, and Jason, an ex-military man, experience a series of criminal jobs that go wrong in the drug-trafficking world of Leonida, a fictional state based on Florida.
According to Rockstar, Leonida is the company's most detailed open world so far, extending beyond Vice City into smaller communities and nightlife hotspots inspired by locations in South Florida.
Music has been an intrinsic part of the GTA experience, and the latest game is expected to feature a soundtrack including artists like Tame Impala and SZA.

items.summary:
🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit
Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it b
items.text:
🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit
Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions.
When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable.
The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things:
- Intimate knowledge of the system
- The drive and determination to force the system to work
Those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure.
Now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse.
And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365, Air Traffic Control, United Airlines' systems, the NSA's network, many major banks, Apple's systems, and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI.
I guess that depends on how you look at it.
I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit.
So where did they go?
Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity.
Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea.
People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from?
It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics.
Smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this.
It's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real.
Thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system).
We've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex an
