items.summary:
US lawmakers push to raise minimum wage to $25, end tipped pay system
Public support for raising the minimum wage grows, with 78 percent of voters saying it was an important election issue.
In Washington, DC, a group of lawmakers has ramped up calls to increase the United States federal minimum wage
items.text:
US lawmakers push to raise minimum wage to $25, end tipped pay system
Public support for raising the minimum wage grows, with 78 percent of voters saying it was an important election issue.
In Washington, DC, a group of lawmakers has ramped up calls to increase the United States federal minimum wage and eliminate the subminimum wage, otherwise known as the tipped wage.
The group of 17 lawmakers, which includes current and newly elected House members, is calling for passage of the Living Wage For All Act, which has been languishing since it was introduced in April.
The legislation’s original lead sponsors include Representative Delia Ramirez of Illinois, Representative Jesus “Chuy” Garcia, also of Illinois, and Representative Analilia Mejia of New Jersey.
The bill aims to gradually raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour, with different timelines depending on the size of the employer.
Brad Lander, a congressman-elect from Brooklyn, New York, who says he will join the bill as a co-sponsor when the next congressional session begins in January, told Al Jazeera: “Doing it federally is the right way to go. Tying it into broader legislation that raises the minimum wage for all workers is a great approach.”
For larger employers — those with more than 500 employees nationwide or at least $1bn in annual revenue — the increase would be completed by 2031. Smaller employers would have until 2038.
After that, the minimum wage would be maintained at two-thirds of the US median hourly wage, with annual adjustments to preserve that ratio.
The bill would also eliminate the separate subminimum wage for tipped workers, currently $2.13 an hour. Under the existing framework, employers can count workers’ tips towards their minimum-wage requirements.
While several states have raised their own minimum wages, the federal rate remains $7.25 an hour, where it has stood since 2009. Washington, DC, has the highest minimum wage of any US jurisdiction, at $18.40 an hour, followed by Washington state at $17.13. However, 20 states do not have a minimum wage higher than the federal rate. Those states include Texas, Georgia and Iowa.
Laws governing the subminimum wage also vary across states. Seven states require employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage before tips, including Alaska, California and Nevada.
Others, including New York, have higher tipped cash wages than the federal rate but allow employers to take a tip credit, meaning they can pay workers less than the standard minimum wage as long as their tips make up the difference.
In New York, minimum wages vary by region. The rate is $17 an hour in New York City and its surrounding suburbs, and $16 an hour in the rest of the state.
For tipped workers outside the food service industry, the minimum cash wage is $14.15 in the New York City metropolitan area and $13.30 elsewhere in the state. For restaurant workers, those rates are $11.35 and $10.70, respectively.
The distinction is a point of contention for Lander.
“All workers deserve a raise. The 45 million working people who make less than $20 an hour deserve a raise, and the tipped subminimum wage is inexcusable at this point,” he said.
A long-term fight
The subminimum wage has long been viewed as a legacy of racial and economic inequalities that disproportionately affected Black Americans. When Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act in 1938, establishing the first federal minimum wage, it excluded categories of workers in domestic and agricultural occupations, which disproportionately employed Black Americans.
Congress extended federal minimum-wage protections to restaurant and other service workers in 1966. But rather than requiring employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage, lawmakers established a separate tipped minimum wage, initially set at 50 percent of the standard federal rate. Employers could count customers’ tips towards the rest of a worker’s minimum-wage obligation. In 1996, Congress froze the federal tipped cash wage at $2.13 an hour, where it remains today.
The purchasing power of the standard federal minimum wage has also changed drastically. Adjusted for inflation, the $7.25 minimum wage in 2009 would be worth $11.32 today, meaning it has lost 36 percent of its purchasing power.
The federal minimum wage’s purchasing power peaked in 1968, when the rate was $1.60 an hour. Adjusted for inflation, that peak would be worth significantly more than the current minimum wage, representing a loss of roughly 53 percent in purchasing power.
The push to raise wages also has public support. A new poll released on Wednesday by One Fair Wage, an organisation that has long campaigned to eliminate the subminimum wage, found that 78 percent of voters considered raising the minimum wage to $25 an hour an important factor in their vote in the recent US midterm elections, where Republicans were dealt massive losses with the cost of living a key issue for voters.
“Washington has allowed the federal minimum wage to become increasingly disconnected from the economic reality facing American families,” Saru Jayaraman, president of One Fair Wage, said in a statement.
The push for the Living Wage For All Act comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and Senate in the new Congress.
The last major attempt to raise the federal minimum wage came during former President Joe Biden’s first year in office. Democrats sought to increase the rate from $7.25 to $15 an hour through the Raise the Wage Act of 2021, which was included in the original proposal for Biden’s American Rescue Plan.
Ultimately, the effort failed after the Senate rejected a motion to waive budgetary rules that would have allowed the minimum-wage increase to proceed. The March 2021 vote was 42–58, with all Republicans opposed, joined by seven Democrats and independent Senator Angus King of Maine, who caucuses with Democrats.
Although the legislation failed, Biden raised the minimum wage for federal contract workers

items.text:
Ukrainian FA to blame for failed drugs test - Mudryk
- Published
On-loan Tottenham winger Mykhailo Mudryk says he blames the administration of the Ukraine national team for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban from football.
The 25-year-old, on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium, which he believes entered his system while on international duty.
Having initially faced a four-year ban from the Football Association (FA), his appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport was successful.
He returned to football after accepting he had breached anti-doping rules and agreeing to a suspension equivalent to the time he had already served.
After appearing for Chelsea during a pre-season tour of Asia, Mudryk joined Tottenham on transfer deadline day to reunite with his former Shakhtar Donetsk manager Roberto de Zerbi.
In a lengthy interview with the Ukrainian YouTube channel Guest of Gordon, Mudryk was asked who he blamed for his absence from the game.
"The environment, the situation in the Ukrainian national team," he replied. "It should never have existed. I probably haven't said it publicly yet, but I'm saying it now.
"I had never heard of a drug like meldonium. It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe. It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England."
He explained how he had only been in Ukraine to be with the national team and "it points to the fact it was in a national team camp".
Asked specifically whether he blamed the national team, Mudryk replied: "Yes, exactly."
He also said Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) president Andriy Shevchenko offered little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and claimed its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.
Mudryk also said he spent millions of pounds on legal fees, coaching, pitch hire and private physiotherapy while being unable to access services at Chelsea.
He added: "It was a bolt from the blue. I couldn't believe it [the positive test] was true.
"It was like falling off a skyscraper. In a dream you would hit the ground. In life, I just kept on falling. It hit me very hard, mentally."
Mudryk said he cried and drank alcohol after the initial suspension but never doubted that he would eventually return to top-level football.
BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.
Last year a UAF spokesperson told BBC Sport it was "in close contact with Mudryk's lawyers" but had not been contacted by the FA about the case.

items.title: US Defence Secretary Hegseth reveals military partnership on Venezuela trip
items.summary:
US Defence Secretary Hegseth reveals military partnership on Venezuela trip
Pete Hegseth says the agreement will include joint training and intelligence sharing with the Venezuelan military.
United States Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth has announced a new agreement with Venezuela’s interim govern
items.text:
US Defence Secretary Hegseth reveals military partnership on Venezuela trip
Pete Hegseth says the agreement will include joint training and intelligence sharing with the Venezuelan military.
United States Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth has announced a new agreement with Venezuela’s interim government to facilitate military cooperation between the two countries.
The Pentagon chief made a surprise visit to the Venezuelan capital of Caracas on Wednesday, becoming the latest in a series of high-level officials under US President Donald Trump to travel to the South American country.
During his stop, Hegseth revealed that the deal would include intelligence sharing and joint training for the two countries’ militaries.
“We see this as a reestablishment of our defence partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries,” he said.
Their shared aim would be “to stabilise Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all”, Hegseth added.
Hegseth was hosted by interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who has led the government since her swearing-in on January 5. His trip was not previously announced by the Pentagon.
The Trump administration has exerted heavy influence over Rodriguez and her government after abducting former President Nicolas Maduro during a military attack on January 3.
Rodriguez was previously Venezuela’s vice president. Trump has justified the attack as a law enforcement effort designed to force Maduro to “stand trial on American soil”, charging him with weapons- and drug-related crimes.
After the operation, Trump also said he planned to “run” Venezuela, and he told The Atlantic magazine that Rodriguez could “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro” if she refuses to comply with US demands.
Since then, he has worked with the Venezuelan government to extract concessions on US priorities such as energy development and military cooperation.
Critics have accused the US of reducing Venezuela to a vassal state and exploiting its resources while leaving Maduro’s government largely intact.
Under Maduro, the Venezuelan state was accused of human rights abuses including torture, arbitrary imprisonment and extrajudicial killings.
Still, Trump has held up Venezuela as a model he would like to see replicated in other countries, like Iran and Cuba.
In Wednesday’s remarks, Hegseth said that the South American country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner”.
Rodriguez hailed the agreement as a “resumption of the technical-military relationship between both countries”, and she expressed hope that their cooperation could be “brought to its highest possible level”.
Hegseth is also set to meet with officials in Colombia later on Wednesday as part of a trip to the region.
Colombian Defence Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora said on Tuesday that the US would deliver a C-130 Hercules military aircraft, as the US steps up military involvement across Latin America.
Hegseth has faced pressure to step down from his role, following a midterm election in which the US-Israel war on Iran contributed to Republican losses across the country.
A key member of Trump’s cabinet, Hegseth has championed the war, as well as efforts to weaken rules of engagement designed to limit civilian casualties.
Hegseth narrowly avoided a recent impeachment effort in the US Congress this month. The sponsor of that effort, outgoing Republican US Representative Thomas Massie, cited the Iran war as well as a campaign of military strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking vessels off the coast of Latin America.
The boat-strike campaign has killed an estimated 244 people and has been denounced as extrajudicial killings by legal experts.

Strasbourg announce appointment of Swans boss Matos

Strasbourg have announced the appointment of Swansea City's Vitor Matos as the club's new head coach.
The French top-flight side made the announcement on Wednesday evening, but there has been no official confirmation of Matos' departure
items.text:
Strasbourg announce appointment of Swans boss Matos
- Published
Strasbourg have announced the appointment of Swansea City's Vitor Matos as the club's new head coach.
The French top-flight side made the announcement on Wednesday evening, but there has been no official confirmation of Matos' departure from the Swans.
Strasbourg are expected to pay Swansea compensation thought to be in the region of £5m in order to secure his services.
Matos, 38, spent just under a year at Swansea having left his role at Maritimo to succeed Alan Sheehan as the Championship club's head coach in November 2025.
Four members of Matos' coaching team - Diogo Medeiros, Toze Mendes, Goncalo Ricca and head of goalkeeping Pedro Pereira - are also expected to leave Swansea.
Ex-captain Ashley Williams is set to return to the club to join an interim coaching team also featuring fellow former players Kristian O'Leary and Leon Britton.
O'Leary and Britton are set to be the only remaining members of Matos' Swansea staff.
Alongside Williams, they will lead Swansea while the club searches for Matos' permanent successor.
Their first game will be at home to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday.
Swansea go to Middlesbrough next Tuesday before hosting rivals Cardiff City on Sunday, 29 November.
Matos moves on despite agreeing an extended Swansea contract running until 2030 in July.
Swansea were 20th in the second tier when the former Liverpool coach took over, but he leaves a team lying only three points off the top of the table in sixth.
Matos led Swansea to an 11th-placed finish last season, and has raised hopes of a potential promotion push in 2026-27 thanks to an encouraging start to this campaign.
But he told Swansea he wanted to move on after Strasbourg, who have the same ownership group as Premier League side Chelsea, made their move last weekend and he said goodbye to players and staff on Tuesday.
Having finished eighth last season, Strasbourg are 13th in Ligue 1 having won only three of their 10 league games under Hugo Oliveira, who was only appointed in the summer after Gary O'Neil departed to take over at Ipswich Town.
Matos was touted as a contender to take charge at Crystal Palace earlier this season - the Eagles have since appointed Thomas Frank - while he had also been linked with a return to Portugal on the back of his impact at Swansea.
When asked in October about the Palace links, Matos said: "I'm Swansea manager. I love being here, love my players, love the staff, so my focus is always on the next game and what we can do better."
In an interview last week, Swansea chief executive Tom Gorringe acknowledged that Matos' impact will not have gone unnoticed at other clubs.
But Gorringe played down the idea of Matos being lured away, saying: "The reality is there'll always be interest in anyone performing well in any role on and off the pitch.
"That's one of the outcomes of being successful - we're aware of that.
"[But] we're all quite happy. We've all agreed to go on this journey together and we hope that Vitor is here a long time."

items.text:
FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on
- Published
The Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, BBC Sport can reveal.
But it believes any attempt to prevent him from standing in the election in March is likely to fail.
Infantino oversaw the introduction of a three-term limit when he replaced Sepp Blatter as leader of world football's governing body.
However, Fifa's council agreed in 2022 that his first period in office from 2016 to 2019 should not count as it was the remainder of his predecessor's interrupted final term.
Earlier this month, human rights campaign group Fair Square wrote to the FA claiming that the decision is open to legal challenge and was "contrary to the spirit and purpose" of Fifa statutes.
It urged the FA to ask Fifa's governance committee to bar Infantino from the election in March because he has already served the maximum three terms.
FA chair Debbie Hewitt has now replied, telling Fair Square that the governing body "has explored the possibility of challenging Mr Infantino's eligibility to run for a further term as the Fifa president but does not consider that such a challenge would secure the outcome sought".
In correspondence seen by the BBC, Hewitt adds: "Ultimately the process followed Fifa's governance and led to an outcome where Mr Infantino's part term was disregarded for the purposes of maximum term limits.
"Having considered the process in detail, we do not believe that a challenge would succeed."
In a statement, Fair Square said: "It's understandable that the FA has no faith in Fifa's internal processes to hold Infantino accountable for serious breaches of the rules, but it's a mistake to abandon these channels, not least because it sends a signal to Infantino that he can do whatever he likes.
"We will encourage the FA to leave its options open where this matter is concerned not least because Debbie Hewitt's position on the Fifa council puts her in a very strong position to demand clear answers on why Fifa discounted Infantino's first term."
Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - has said a national association or confederation may need to challenge Infantino's eligibility at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).
The FA was among a number of national associations to withdraw its support of Infantino in the wake of the crisis sparked by his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.
European confederation Uefa has backed rival candidate Philippe Diallo, the president of the French Football Federation.
Hewitt, who became a member of Fifa's council in 2023, also told Fair Square that the FA "remains opposed to Mr Infantino's re-election and is committed to providing its full support to Philippe Diallo as our preferred candidate in the upcoming Fifa presidential election".
Fifa has been approached for comment.
It has previously referred to the fact that in 2022 its council "unanimously confirmed its agreement with the view of the governance, audit & compliance committee that the period between 2016 and 2019 does not count as a term of office for the current Fifa president, who is therefore about to end his first term".
The FA declined to comment.

What does Israel’s new ground offensive mean for Palestinians in Gaza?

Israeli forces have launched a ground operation in central Gaza, advancing west of the line they wi
items.text:
What does Israel’s new ground offensive mean for Palestinians in Gaza?
Israeli tanks advance beyond the ‘Yellow Line’, forcing Palestinians to flee again as Gaza faces a deepening humanitarian crisis.
Israeli forces have launched a ground operation in central Gaza, advancing west of the line they withdrew to under last year’s ceasefire and forcing Palestinian families, many of whom had already been displaced, to flee their homes once again.
The operation, the first major ground offensive publicly announced by the Israeli military since the ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025, follows a warning by the United States-backed Board of Peace that the 13-month-old agreement risks collapse. In a report to the United Nations Security Council, the board accused Israel of restricting aid and delaying the deployment of Palestinian police, and Hamas of continuing armed activity and taxing goods entering Gaza. Senior Hamas official Basem Naim dismissed the report as “pure disinformation”.
What happened in central Gaza on Wednesday?
Israeli tanks and bulldozers advanced towards Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south route, east of the Nuseirat refugee camp and north of the Bureij refugee camp, Al Jazeera correspondents reported. Palestinians fled those areas, amid heavy gunfire and artillery shelling.
The Israeli military body overseeing civilian affairs in the occupied Palestinian territory, known as COGAT, said the army had closed that stretch of Salah al-Din Street and told residents to stay away until further notice. The army hasn’t said how long the operation will last.
An Israeli attack on al-Mughraqa killed one person and wounded several others, an official at al-Awda Hospital told Al Jazeera. Separate attacks in Deir el-Balah, Nuseirat and Gaza City killed three more people.
“We fear this may be the start of a broader operation and that displacement will begin anew, as we have not yet recovered from the effects of the previous war and displacement,” Mahmoud al-Saafin, a 27-year-old resident of Bureij, told the AFP news agency.
The areas targeted in the operation lie west of the “Yellow Line”, where Israeli troops pulled back to under the first phase of President Donald Trump’s plan, leaving them in about 53 percent of Gaza. Israel has, however, continued to move that line gradually, and it now encompasses around two-thirds of the enclave. More than two million Palestinians live in the rest, mostly in tents.
Why does Israel say it launched the operation?
The military told AFP it had launched “a precise operation” west of the line “to remove a threat” posed to the Israeli army, adding that “there is Hamas infrastructure in the area, adding it was responding to Hamas ceasefire violations.
“We reserve the freedom to act and manoeuvre whenever necessary to eliminate any immediate threat in the Gaza Strip,” the army said.
Israel says Hamas has been regrouping and rearming, and it has stepped up attacks. On Saturday, an Israeli attack killed Samir Abu Younis, the Qassam Brigades’ Rafah commander.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel won’t withdraw until Hamas is dismantled. “If tensions escalate on the various fronts, we are fully prepared to seize additional territory, evacuate local residents and incorporate it into Israel’s permanent security perimeter,” he said.
How have Palestinian groups, including Hamas, responded?
Hamas called the operation and the forced evacuations northeast of Nuseirat “a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement”, and urged mediators to “intervene immediately”.
It accused Israel of “systematically” squeezing Palestinians into a narrow area of Gaza, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s caretaker government of escalating to escape its domestic crises.
Hamas also condemned the Board of Peace for having “unacceptably equated the occupation’s ongoing aggression with the suffering of the Palestinian victim”.
The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine called the operation a “prelude” to a wider escalation aimed at forcibly displacing Palestinians.
Has Israel violated the Gaza ceasefire before?
Israeli forces have kept up near-daily attacks, shelling and home demolitions. Gaza’s Ministry of Health says they have killed 1,658 Palestinians and wounded 6,000 since the ceasefire began. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in the same period, the Reuters news agency reports.
On Tuesday alone, Israeli fire killed six Palestinians, including a six-year-old boy, Gaza’s civil defence agency and hospitals told AFP.
Aid remains restricted. About 100,000 tents are waiting to enter Gaza, held up by crossing closures and lengthy Israeli security checks, the International Organization for Migration says.
Where does the ceasefire stand?
The ceasefire halted major fighting, but the rest of the plan, covering Israel’s withdrawal, reconstruction and Hamas’s disarmament, has stalled. Hamas agreed in July to a roadmap to give up its weapons and hand over governance. Israel rejected it.
Israel also hasn’t let the board’s technocratic administration start work in Gaza. That has held up an international stabilisation force, The Associated Press news agency reported.
The board spelled out what failure would mean. “Should it collapse, there would be no road map to return to, no administration to deploy and no enabling environment to rebuild.”

The research org
items.text:
Pew Research: Islam on track to become world’s largest religion by 2035
The report projects steady increases for both Christianity and Islam from 2020 to 2070.
Islam will soon be the world’s largest religion, taking Christianity’s place by 2035, according to the Pew Research Center.
The research organisation assessed the Muslim population’s expected growth in a report released on Tuesday, which projected that both groups will see their numbers increase over the next few decades.
However, the Muslim population will “simply [grow] at a faster pace,” the report said.
The projection analysed 201 countries and territories, accounting for 99.98 percent of the population, and spanned the geographic distribution and future changes of seven religious groups and affiliations – Muslims, Christians, Jews, Hindus, Buddhists, and others – from the years 2020 to 2070.
The results are part of the Pew-Templeton Global Religious Futures Project, which seeks to analyse religious change and its impact on the world.
The organisation stressed that the findings are “not intended to predict all the ways the world could change” as several other events might occur that could impact a group’s religious affiliation, such as socioeconomic circumstances, natural disasters, and wars.
Baby boom
According to the report, Muslims give birth to the highest number of children, one of the factors that Pew says make them the world’s fastest-growing religious group.
Fertility rates were found to be 3.1 children per Muslim woman, while Christians, with the second-highest fertility rate, had 2.5 children per Christian woman.
A generation can typically replace itself with a fertility rate of around 2.1 children per woman.
Both groups are expected to “keep pace with the world’s overall population growth”, according to Pew.
Muslims could gain up to 1.6 billion people through natural population change, compared to 792 million people for Christians.
Estimated losses
Muslims are expected to have much smaller losses in their community than Christians leaving or converting religions.
“The difference between the number of people who join and leave Islam is expected to result in a loss of 8 million people during the projection period, [whereas] for Christians, the net difference is a projected loss of 105 million people,” the report said.
Those who choose to depart from Christianity may not identify with a religion afterwards, including atheists and agnostics.
However, the research finds that Islam’s projected growth is not the result of people converting from Christianity: the number of Muslims projected to convert to Christianity is only “slightly greater” than the number of Christians expected to become Muslims.
Country dynamics
Between 2020 and 2070, “most of the growth in the world’s Muslim population is projected to occur in places where Muslims already make up a majority of the population”, said Pew.
By 2070, Muslims will make up 95 percent of the population in the Middle East-North Africa region. Meanwhile, in the Asia-Pacific region, Muslims are expected to surpass the religiously unaffiliated.
Muslims were the majority religious group in 53 countries in 2020. An additional 1.2 billion Muslims are expected to live in these countries by 2070, representing 74 percent of the projected growth of the global Muslim population.
For instance, Pakistan’s Muslim population is expected to double from 227 million in 2020 to 461 million in 2070. The country will become the world’s largest Muslim population, overtaking Indonesia, Pew said.
Christian growth will also be concentrated across 120 countries where Christians were already the majority of the population.
Overall, the population of Christians in these countries is forecast to rise by 630 million, representing 92 percent of global Christian growth.

items.text:
What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
November 18, 2026
It had been a year and a half since Ukraine last attacked the 19-kilometer-long Kerch Bridge connecting Russian-annexed Crimea with Russia's Krasnodar region.
Now, Ukraine has struck again. The attack during the night of November 17 caused the highway section of the bridge to collapse into the sea. As a result, shipping traffic between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov has also been disrupted.
Russia's ministry of transport announced a "temporary suspension" of road and rail traffic on the bridge, though later, rail services were resumed. Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into what they are calling a "terrorist attack." It was only after this announcement that the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) confirmed the attack.
The Kerch Strait bridge is considered one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prestigious projects. Its construction began after Russia's 2014 annexation of the Ukrainian Crimea peninsula, an act considered illegal under international law. The Kerch Bridge was completed four years later.
It has been targeted by Ukraine on several occasions since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion. The most well-known strike occurred in October 2022, when an explosives-laden truck detonated on the bridge, causing extensive damage and several months of traffic restrictions. The most recent attack took place in June 2025, when the SBU reported that an underwater support structure was blown up.
A long time in the making
The latest Ukrainian operation lasted about a month, and consisted of seven distinct phases. "First, the SBU and armed forces systematically neutralized the enemy's air defense system. After that, the direct attack on the bridge began," says the SBU Telegram channel.
Some Russian military bloggers claim that the attack was carried out with the support of Ukraine's Western allies, or at least using their equipment and weapons.
Ukraine has not confirmed this. It has instead pointed out that various Ukrainian-made weapons were used in the attack, ranging from a variety of drones, to FP-5 Flamingo and R-360 Neptun missiles. British daily The Times has cited Ukrainian military sources, saying that Ukraine attacked the bridge without the support of SpaceX's satellite network system Starlink. There has been no confirmation of this so far.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, described the strike as a response to Russian attacks: "Russia is attacking our infrastructure every day, particularly bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region." He said "we are rebuilding our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that the war always returns to where it began."
The impact on shipping
After the attack, pictures and videos of the bridge were shared on social media. The Krimskij Veter Telegram channel has highlighted damage to the railroad link and questioned why Russian authorities have opted to resume train services.
The Kerch Strait shipping channel is also completely blocked by debris. "This brings road traffic to a standstill, but also shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov," the channel writes.
Indeed, the Kerch Strait navigational channel is merely 120 meters wide, writes Mychajlo Hontschar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" on Facebook. "The strait is shallow, only three to five meters deep."
As early as the 19th century, the seabed was dredged to allow heavier ships to pass from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov and vice versa. "Now, Vladimir Putin's bridge-building efforts have brought shipping to an indefinite standstill," Hontschar said.
Not only will river-sea vessels no longer be able to leave the waters of the Sea of Azov, the Don, and the Volga, but boats and small ships from the Black Sea fleet and the Caspian flotilla based in Novorossiysk will also be unable to do so.
The military consequences
Many pro-Kremlin Telegram channels have been quick to claim that the bridge does not play an important role in the Russian army's logistics or in supplying Crimea.
The Dva Mayora (Two Majors) channel quotes the "Deputy President of the Republic of Crimea," Olga Kurlayeva, who described the bridge as a "purely civilian structure."
Ukrainian military experts interviewed by DW, on the other hand, point to the systematic disruption of Russian logistics. These efforts also included regular attacks on the R-80 highway leading through Russian-occupied territories of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
Russia cannot replace the Kerch Bridge with any other land connection, says Oleksandr Kovalenko, a Ukrainian military expert with the Information Resistance Group that seeks to counter disinformation. He expects the damaged bridge will cause supply problems for the Russian armed forces: "If there is a resource shortage during attacks or in defense, then either the attacks or the defense will fail."
That is why he does not rule out a decline in attacks from occupied Crimea on the rest of Ukraine. "There are many launch pads for kamikaze drones in Crimea — in the Hvardijsk area, at Cape Chauda and in Balaklava," Kovalenko told DW. "From there, many drones are launched toward Odesa, Mykolaiv, and the right bank of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region. They also fly over Crimea en route toward Ukraine. Then there are attacks using Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as Zircon and Oniks missiles, guided missiles, and glide bombs. And while they don't originate in Crimea, they are brought over via the Kerch Bridge."
A bad look for Putin
Kovalenko says the bridge strike has dealt a serious blow to Vladimir Putin's standing. It comes at a sensitive time as Putin is about to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen, China.
Memes and witty comments about the bridge abound on X. Meanwhile, the Russian president's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has promised to rebuild the bridge and assured that it wi

items.title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military
items.summary:
Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.
Maduro was controversially seized by
items.text:
Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.
Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.
Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela. Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.
“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.
In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.
“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.
Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.
“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.
During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.
But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”
Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.
Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.
“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.
Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”
Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.
But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Venezuela on Wednesday, met with the country's interim authorities and also signed a military cooperation deal with the Latin American country.
What do we know so far about Hegseth'
items.text:
US Pentagon chief Hegseth signs military deal in Venezuela
November 18, 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Venezuela on Wednesday, met with the country's interim authorities and also signed a military cooperation deal with the Latin American country.
What do we know so far about Hegseth's trip?
The Pentagon did not release any information on Hegseth's trip or confirm the visit, although it was broadcast on Venezuelan state media.
The visit comes after US forces in January ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and took him along with his wife to New York to face drug trafficking charges. Since then, US President Donald Trump has backed acting President Delcy Rodriguez to lead the country.
Both Rodriguez and Hegseth touted the new military agreement between the two countries at the presidential palace in Caracas.
Rodriguez said the deal would strengthen training for the Venezuelan military while facilitating access to new technologies. She said this would allow the two nations to "face common threats."
Hegseth said the US sees the deal "as a reestablishment of our defense partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries."
The agreement includes intelligence sharing between the two nations in addition to joint training.
The Pentagon chief said the US seeks "to ensure the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors or narco-terrorists or criminals and that they are safe and secure inside sovereign borders."
Hegseth said Wednesday that since Maduro's ouster, Venezuela "has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner."
How have US-Venezuela relations changed?
US-Venezuela relations were strained under Maduro, who had taken office in 2013. In 2019, Maduro cut off Venezuela's formal diplomatic relations with the US after Trump's first administration recognized Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaido as the country's interim president.
After the ouster of Maduro, the Trump administration urged Venezuela to comply with demands such as US access to the Venezuelan oil market. Trump had threatened Rodriguez, who was Venezuela's vice president, with a "fate worse than Maduro" if she didn't cooperate with Washington.
Trump has later praised Rodriguez as a "terrific person" who is doing a "great job."
Under Rodriguez, Venezuela has released political prisoners and facilitated the shipments of oil to the US, with the US then controlling the proceeds and returning the money under an energy deal. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been overseeing Venezuela's transition and is in close contact with Rodriguez.
Elections after Maduro's ouster are expected at some point in Venezuela, but with Rodriguez's government acting favorably towards the US, it's unclear whether they would happen anytime soon. Nobel Prize winner and opposition leader Maria Corina Machado recently urged elections after arriving in Venezuela.

Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee c
items.text:
Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
- Published
Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.
Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.
It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.
Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
- Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show 
  - Published16 January
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The Israeli military said the first two strikes targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third incident, according to AFP news agency.
At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Democratic lawmakers have opened a probe into whether United States Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick used his position to help Can
items.text:
US lawmakers launch probe into Lutnick’s actions amid Nvidia scandal
Letter alleges possible conflict of interest in Lutnick not adding Megaspeed to US trade blacklist.
Democratic lawmakers have opened a probe into whether United States Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick used his position to help Cantor Fitzgerald, an investment firm controlled by his two sons, avoid financial losses amid the scandal involving Jensen Huang at artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia.
In the five-page letter dated November 17, House Democrats notified Brandon Lutnick, chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald and Howard Lutnick’s son, that they are requesting information to ascertain whether “any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.
Al Jazeera has reviewed the letter.
The letter was authored by Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who is the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, Gregory Meeks of New York and the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California. It asks if the company’s financial exposure influenced Lutnick’s decision to keep Megaspeed off the US Entity List, a trade blacklist.
Megaspeed is attached to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who reportedly had an affair with now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week.
The US adds companies to the Entity List if it determines they pose a risk to US national security or foreign policy.
“The Secretary has fully complied with the terms of his ethics agreement, including all divestiture and recusal requirements, and will continue to do so. He has divested all financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald, Newmark, and BGC,” a Commerce Department spokesperson said in a statement in response to the letter, which was first reported by the Financial Times.
Cantor Fitzgerald denied the claims in the letter, saying it holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia. Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients, according to the Reuters news agency.
The firm also said it has no role in US export control or Entity List decisions.
Earlier this month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said four government agencies had favoured putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist, but the Commerce Department, which was in charge, had not.
Reuters also reported that senior White House officials have discussed whether Lutnick should be pushed out.
On Tuesday, Huang, in his first public statement after he stepped down from Nvidia, said he would be “honored” to return as CEO, but the company’s board during its earnings call later in the day ruled out bringing him back.

Washington, DC, USA – United States President Donald Trump is set to hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday i
items.text:
Trump and Putin to meet one-on-one in China Thursday
Coordinated US diplomatic effort underway to end the war in Ukraine, a US official tells Al Jazeera.
Washington, DC, USA – United States President Donald Trump is set to hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, a US official tells Al Jazeera.
The two presidents last met in Alaska in August 2025 for high-stakes negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, but failed to reach a settlement.
The US official said on Wednesday that, in addition to the president’s engagements in China, American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to meet with Ukrainian officials and European partners in Berlin on Thursday to develop post-war security guarantees and a comprehensive economic recovery plan for Kyiv.
“The Berlin meetings and President Trump’s engagements in China are part of a coordinated diplomatic effort,” the official said.
“President Trump remains committed to ending the fighting and the tremendous human suffering, while helping establish the conditions for a sovereign, secure and prosperous Ukraine.”
On Thursday, Trump and Putin are also scheduled to join their Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, for an unprecedented trilateral summit on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen, marking the first-ever gathering of the leaders of the world’s three major powers.

items.text:
Valtteri Bottas: Cadillac confirm Finnish driver to stay with team for 2027 Formula 1 season ahead of Las Vegas Grand Prix
Valtteri Bottas will remain with Cadillac next year after speculation his future at the team was in doubt; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with Friday's practice sessions at 12.30am and 4pm
Wednesday 18 November 2026 20:14, UK
Cadillac have confirmed Valtteri Bottas will stay on at the team for the 2027 Formula 1 season, ending speculation about the Finnish driver's future.
Bottas returned after a year's absence from the grid for this season, Cadillac's first in the sport, as one of two hugely experienced drivers for the all-new American team's first line-up alongside Sergio Perez, who signed a contract extension last month until at least 2029.
But, Bottas' future has been up in the air recently as Cadillac pushed for American Formula 2 driver Colton Herta to earn a Formula 1 super licence, which he secured two weeks ago, by running him in practice sessions.
- Las Vegas GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports

- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
The team have committed to Bottas for another year though, citing the 37-year-old's "extensive Formula 1 experience, technical insight and race-winning pedigree to the team".
"To whom it may concern, I'm staying!" said Bottas, in reference to his team radio after winning the 2019 Australian Grand Prix with Mercedes.
"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027. We knew building a new Formula 1 team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.
"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come, I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."
Newcomers Cadillac are yet to score a point in their maiden campaign but Bottas is ahead of Perez in the Drivers' Championship due to countback, as his 13th place result at the Chinese Grand Prix is the team's highest result.
But, Perez has generally outpaced his team-mate which, with the links of Cadillac potentially keen for an American driver in Herta, led to speculation about Bottas' future.
Cadillac F1 CEO Dan Towriss said: "Valtteri's experience, perspective and commitment are important strengths for our team.
"Continuity gives us a strong platform as we continue developing the team and working toward our ambitions in Formula 1. On the eve of the Las Vegas GP, everyone in the team is pleased to have Valtteri locked in for 2027 alongside Checo and look forward to the next stage of our journey together."
Cadillac say they will announce their 2027 F1 reserve and test drivers in "due course".
Just one seat left to be filled on 2027 F1 grid
With Bottas' future secured and Racing Bulls confirming last week that Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will be their line-up once again in 2027, only Haas are yet to complete their driver pairing for next year.
Last month, Haas announced Rafael Camara will drive for the team in 2027, having already made an early F1 debut in Brazil and will compete again this weekend in Las Vegas, after Esteban Ocon was dropped following a dispute at the Mexico City Grand Prix.
But, Oliver Bearman has not been confirmed, although is expected to keep his seat once a "few bigger-picture things that we're working on" have been resolved according to the British driver.
Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu furiously dismissed reports claiming that contract extension talks with Bearman are being held up by the British driver demanding a £5m annual salary.
"I have no idea where that comes from," he said in Mexico.
"I've experienced this sometimes this season as well. People say there's no smoke without fire but really some people will invent a story."

Narendra Modi thanked Prince William for bringing his Earthshot prize to the country during the couple's first int
items.text:
William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour
- Published
The Prince and Princess of Wales have met India's prime minister as they ended their three-day visit to the country.
Narendra Modi thanked Prince William for bringing his Earthshot prize to the country during the couple's first international tour since 2022.
It comes a day after the royal couple gave out £1m prizes to winners of the environmental award, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.
Catherine also visited a maternity hospital, where she comforted a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls.
On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.
During a meeting at Modi's private residence, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".
The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.
Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the UK–India partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".
When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.
The royal spokesperson said that the meeting with Modi touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".
The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known filmmakers.
The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.
Ahead of their meeting with Modi on Wednesday, William met with film stars during a visit to a film production company, while Catherine visited a maternity hospital, where she met grieving mother Jyoti Karande.
Karande, whose other child remains in intensive care, is receiving treatment in the post-partum ward at Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital.
Catherine told the 29-year-old: "Stay strong. Well done. You've clearly been very, very brave."
William and Catherine's first official overseas trip in four years was short, but allowed them to combine personal projects - like Earthshot - with diplomacy.
As the future king and queen, they are viewed as a valuable diplomatic asset by the UK government.
And with Catherine recovering well and back on international duties following her cancer treatment, visits of a similar kind can be expected to fill their calendar.

items.title: Sam Altman says his life is so weird that he’s unfazed by Andrew Garfield portraying him in upcoming movie
items.summary:
Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years.
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thu
items.text:
Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years.
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thursday to tell the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the downfall of FTX.
As the founder and CEO of OpenAI, one of the most influential companies of the century, Sam Altman isn’t going to escape the Hollywood treatment, either.
In “Artificial,” a biographical comedy-drama opening in theaters on Christmas, the lauded actor Andrew Garfield will portray Altman in a film that chronicles OpenAI’s rise and the internal turmoil that erupted when he was briefly ousted in 2023.
“If you had told me 20 years ago that someone was going to make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as … that would have been a very weird thing,” Altman said onstage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “Now it doesn’t feel like it’s in like the top 10 weirdest things about my life.”
Garfield is best known for his role as Spider-Man, but his big break came in 2010, when he played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” alongside Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. (That film also had a sequel of sorts this year called “The Social Reckoning,” but it bombed at the box office.)
So, if Altman isn’t fazed by the looming release of “Artificial,” what’s actually the weirdest thing in his life?
“The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we have, we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well,” Altman said. “That’s a crazy situation to find yourself in.”
Sure, that is pretty weird, Sam. It’s also weird that you use ChatGPT for parenting advice and don’t respect olive oil. But I’d wager to say it’s even weirder that there’s an upcoming film about the time your colleagues briefly ousted you because they were concerned that you can’t be trusted.
Say what you want about Mark Zuckerberg (I certainly have), but at least he’s honest about what he thinks about “The Social Network.”
“It was weird, man,” Zuckerberg reflected on a podcast last year. “They got all these very specific details of what I was wearing, or these specific things correct, but then the whole narrative arc around my motivations and all this stuff were like, completely wrong … The whole arc is like, I’m somehow motivated by trying to find a girlfriend, [but] I was dating Priscilla [Chan] before I started Facebook.”
Zuckerberg said he knew his employees would be tempted to see the movie, so he organized a company outing when it was released, even though the film hardly paints a flattering portrait of him.
Zuckerberg even had enough of a sense of humor to buy a prop from the film at auction. He owns an Ardsley High School T-shirt that Eisenberg wore in the movie and even wore it himself in a video with YouTubers Colin and Samir.
Eisenberg hasn’t been particularly complimentary of Zuckerberg, saying that he doesn’t want to think of himself as “associated with somebody like that.” And while “Artificial” hasn’t hit theaters yet, Garfield doesn’t seem to have a much more favorable opinion of the tech founder he portrays.
“I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield told Esquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a company or technology that you know is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.”

items.title: ‘An honour’: Pochettino up for challenge of leading Manchester United revival
items.summary:
Mauricio Pochettino said it was “an honour” and “a privilege” to be the new Manchester United head coach after arriving in England on Wednesday.
Pochettino flew from Cincinnati to Manchester overnight after overseeing the USA beating Haiti in his final game in charge. Members of Pochettino’s staff l
items.text:
Mauricio Pochettino said it was “an honour” and “a privilege” to be the new Manchester United head coach after arriving in England on Wednesday.
Pochettino flew from Cincinnati to Manchester overnight after overseeing the USA beating Haiti in his final game in charge. Members of Pochettino’s staff landed earlier in the week to begin work at Carrington, laying the foundations as United seek to turn their season around. His right-hand man, Jesús Pérez, the goalkeeping coach Toni Jiménez and the fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino, who continues to work with his father, have already taken training with those not on international duty.
Those away with their national teams will return to the club on Thursday, when they are expected to meet Pochettino for the first time and hold meetings. Conversations have also been held with various departments within the club, as Pochettino sought to learn about the squad’s health as he seeks areas of improvement.
Pochettino’s first challenge will be at Anfield on Sunday, when 18th-placed United take on Liverpool. The 54-year-old has his eyes set on rattling Manchester City after being told on TNT Sports that “Manchester’s blue and always will be blue” by DaMarcus Beasley, who once had a loan spell with City. Pochettino responded: “No way. You will see. Give me time … give me time and that is going to start to change.”
Speaking about joining United, Pochettino said: “It’s a big challenge but at the same time, it’s adrenaline that you want to feel because I think we are going to have a different job. But I think one of the things that is important is that we have the experience to deal with that, and I think we need to add our common sense and the way we are going to approach all the things.
“We know that the situation is not a situation that a club like Manchester United deserves,” Pochettino added. “The fanbase is amazing and after we signed here in America, of every 10 people I crossed in the street, nine are Manchester United fans. It’s amazing.”
Pochettino is also reunited with the strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya, the analyst Alec Scott and his long-term assistant, Miki D’Agostino, at Old Trafford.

items.title: Snapchat now lets developers build AR Lenses with AI assistants like Claude Code and Cursor
items.summary: Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearan
items.text:
Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera.
The company is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same idea into developers’ existing workflows, allowing AI assistants to handle the technical work while creators focus on the vision for the Lens itself.
The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants. Instead of requiring creators to learn how to use Snapchat’s own development tools, the company is bringing Lens creation into the AI coding workflows they already use, which could in turn expand the pool of people who build for Snapchat.
Developers enrolled in Snapchat’s Lens+ Payouts program can earn from the Lenses they create with Easy Lens CLI. Snapchat says it paid out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month.
Lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat says. That includes building with more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, and publishing them to Snapchat and tracking their performance.
With Easy Lens CLI, Snapchat says developers can create everything from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera effects and beauty filters.
AI assistants can generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to the creator’s phone. The new capability can take a game from an initial idea to a published Lens in a single day, without developers having to write code themselves, Snapchat says.
The tool is aimed at different types of creators. The company notes that game developers can bring existing browser games to Snapchat as Web Lenses, while AI creators can use assets from their preferred tools to build Lenses in their own style. Additionally, agencies and brands can turn existing campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time.
Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.

François Picard is pleased to welcome Israeli writer and filmmaker Etgar Keret, author of "The Seven Good Years", joining us from Tel Aviv. Keret argues that Netanyahu is seeking to remain in power, at any cost, including delegitimizing Arab parties and prolonging conflict. “For him, it could be a never-ending war as long as he's in power. He has no incentive to stop it,” he warns. Keret also calls for Israelis to examine how the war in Gaza was conducted, arguing that “the media as a whole ignored the war.”
Asked whether such reflection and introspection could be possible without Netanyahu, he replies: “I believe, and the reason that I use the word ‘believe’ is that I do not know.” Despite his criticism of the country's leadership, Keret says he has not given up on Israel. Recalling his parents, both Holocaust survivors, he explains: “They didn't dream of Netanyahu.” For now, he intends to remain: “As long as I feel that there is hope, then I'm here to stay and to try to make a difference.”

items.text:
Brooks Koepka: American labels his 2026 PGA Tour season a 'disappointment' and targets 2027 Ryder Cup spot
Brooks Koepka will tee up in the RSM Classic this weekend; the American left LIV Golf in 2025 and returned to the PGA Tour earlier this year but has endured a tough season; watch the RSM Classic live on Sky Sports Golf
Wednesday 18 November 2026 20:21, UK
Brooks Koepka has dubbed his 2026 season a "a disappointment" but insists he is hungry to secure a spot on Team USA's 2027 Ryder Cup squad.
The American returned to the PGA Tour via the one-time-only Returning Member Program in January following his LIV Golf exit at the end of 2025, a decision he said he was "beyond happy with".
After being welcomed back to the tour with open arms, Koepka made his return at the Farmers Insurance Open in February. He'd go on to make 16 starts on the PGA Tour this year but would miss the cut at five events and record only one top-10 finish.

Koepka, who was not selected as one of Keegan Bradley's captain's picks for the 2025 Ryder Cup and was also omitted from Brandt Snedeker's President's Cup team in 2026, hopes to raise his game and earn a spot in the roster for next year's Ryder Cup.
"Adare Manor is a big goal of mine," Koepka said. "But this year has just been a little bit of a disappointment, so I know I need to pick it up a little bit.
"It's something I don't enjoy, sitting back watching the Presidents Cup.
"I know I've only played in one [2017], a lot of those [omissions are due to] injuries. But those team events are a lot of fun, I really enjoy them.
"Getting to be around the guys and representing your country is pretty cool.
"So, anytime you can do that, or you have the opportunity to, and you're not able to go play, it kind of infuriates me sitting on the sidelines."
The 36-year-old has featured in four Ryder Cup's in the past, notably helping Team USA to victory in at Hazletine in 2016 and Whistling Straits in 2020.
He boasts an overall individual record of 7-6-2.
'The reception was fantastic from the players'
Koepka was the lone player to elect to sign up to the PGA Tour's Returning Member Program, with Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith all snubbing the deal, instead choosing to remain at LIV Golf in 2026.
However, following the dissolution of the formerly Saudi-backed breakaway league, Rahm, DeChambeau and Smith have all elected to rejoin the DP World Tour for the 2027 season, along with multiple other former LIV Golf players.
Koepka, meanwhile, was asked ahead of this week's RSM Classic whether he felt back at home after returning to the PGA Tour, replying: "Yeah, I felt very at peace with coming back.
"The reception was fantastic from all the players, caddies, just everybody on tour.
"I think I kept a good relationship with everybody even when I left.
"I think that played probably a huge part in that.
"Everybody was really receptive. I loved the conversations that I've had just throughout the year, just guys asking what was going on, thought process and how things went and the decisions made to get back here.
"Everything was great. I'm beyond happy with my decision."
Can Koepka win the RSM Classic? Watch the first round of the PGA Tour event live on Sky Sports Golf from 1.30pm on Thursday.

You can strike Jensen Huang from the guest list but good luck steering dinner conversation away from the topic in Shenzhen. The co-founder of the AI computing leader was to accompany the US president to the APEC summit before he was undone by revelations of a dalliance with a Chinese national that happened to coincide with a Singapore client's backdoor skirting of sanctions on its powerful H200 chips.
We’ll ask about the fallout and the subsequent tightening of restrictions on US exports of chips to China, the infighting within the Trump administration and whether Huang’s demise marks a high point in Silicon Valley’s bid to quickly corner the market on artificial intelligence. A comeuppance for the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic one day before its launch on the stock market? Or will the United States simply double down on export restrictions and impose its will where it can? What consequences in the host city of the summit, Shenzhen home to huge homegrown tech and industry champions but also for instance the Chinese headquarters of US retail giant Walmart? Summits can assuage some of the planet's biggest fears. But how did we get from a world where that biggest fear was nuclear proliferation to one where it’s artificial intelligence?
