items.title: How fallen giants and their fans bounce back from scandal -- and relegation
items.summary:
What does it feel like to realize the club you love is stuck in a doom spiral of its own making?
Whether due to cheating, financial mismanagement or general ineptitude, some of Europe's greatest teams have suffered the ignominy of relegation by means of punishment -- and their supporters have watche
items.text:
What does it feel like to realize the club you love is stuck in a doom spiral of its own making?
Whether due to cheating, financial mismanagement or general ineptitude, some of Europe's greatest teams have suffered the ignominy of relegation by means of punishment -- and their supporters have watched it unfold. From Juventus and Fiorentina in Italy to Rangers in Scotland, fans have seen offices stripped bare and managers and players scrambling for places on the first boats off the sinking ship.
But a crisis offers the chance for heroes to drag their team out of the deep while suits swap seats in the boardrooms. And amid schadenfreude, anger and denial, supporters of flawed giants find unity through their morbid, self-deprecating humor and fortitude in their situation.
As Manchester City's fans await the results of their appeal and the level of punishment for their 114 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, they might find some small comfort in seeing how others have bounced back from the depths of despair ... or renewed dread at the tribulations that could lie ahead.
Fleeing for greener pastures
By the time manager Fabio Capello had sprinted to Real Madrid in 2006, taking stars Emerson and Fabio Cannavaro with him, Juventus' offices had already been ransacked.
The "Calciopoli" scandal started as a doping investigation into Juventus, but instead found evidence of attempted match-fixing by executives who manipulated referees and their bosses -- a scandal that also implicated Fiorentina, AC Milan, Reggina and Lazio. Papers, contracts and hard drives were seized by the Guardia di Finanza (Financial Police) on May 18, 2006.
The original swath of punishments was handed out just six days after Italy won the 2006 World Cup. Juventus were hammered the hardest; they were kicked down to Serie B and stripped of their 2005 and 2006 league titles, triggering a flurry of expedited exit strategies.
"This world had been turned upside down," Ibrahimovic wrote in his 2011 autobiography. "It wasn't possible to take it all in. We'd won two titles in a row -- were we going to lose everything? One after one the players got away ... every one of us who were left called our agents: 'Sell us, sell us.'
"Uncertainty and desperation hung in the air ... No way was I going to sacrifice a year in the second division. My best years were in danger of being wasted; I told [agent Mino Raiola], 'Do whatever it takes, just get me out of here.'"
Ibrahimovic watched teammates Lilian Thuram and Gianluca Zambrotta join Barcelona, while Patrick Vieira headed to Internazionale. Didier Deschamps took charge, though he couldn't persuade Ibrahimovic to stay. Ibrahimovic said he'd train but wouldn't play in matches, leading to the striker refusing to get on the bus for a preseason game -- instead, he hid in his room and played video games, eventually joining Vieira at Inter.
"In the years following the scandal, any player who had left Juventus and came back to play would get booed. The fans felt betrayed," Lorenzo Bettoni, Football Italia editor, told ESPN. "Even today, if they come back to the Allianz Stadium, they'll still get booed."
Gianluigi Buffon, Alessandro del Piero, Pavel Nedved and David Trézéguet remained and guided Juventus through Serie B. "We chose to stay together to honour a shirt, a club, a fanbase," Buffon wrote in a column for La Stampa in 2017. "We lost everything to gain things which aren't measurable and can't be bartered: respect, affection."
AC Milan's players feared relegation, too. "The whole thing was an absolute shambles," Andrea Pirlo wrote in "I Think Therefore I Play." "One thing I was sure of, though: I would never drop down to Serie B. And if I had to leave, I wouldn't feel like a traitor. You always want to be ambitious and play for a noble cause. There was no way I was going to pay for other people's sins, if that's what they turned out to be." Ultimately, Milan received a hefty points deduction but remained in Serie A.
Choosing to stay
While some players seek the nearest exit option, others choose to stay. Their club's careworn fans hold them close as symbols of hope and rare loyalty.
When Fiorentina were declared bankrupt due to unpaid debts and wages and dissolved in summer 2002, the club restarted in the fourth tier as a brand-new entity. Italy international Angelo Di Livio, then 36, refused to flee and joined the phoenix club Associazione Calcio Fiorentina e Florentia Viola. On June 18, 2002, Di Livio was a second-half substitute as Italy were knocked out of the World Cup by South Korea. Three months later, he started for the reformed Fiorentina team as they drew 1-1 at Sangiovannese in the fourth tier of Italian football.
"My other teammates left, but I stayed in [Florence] for a few days to reflect with my family," Di Livio said in an interview with La Nazione. "Then I called [sporting director] Giovanni Galli and said, 'If you want, count on me. I'm staying.'
"I owed it to the Viola fans. In this city there has always been a true, authentic passion. And there was a great desire for rebirth." His 2003 memoir -- part of a great swath of Fiorentina-related literature -- was called "Io resto qui" ("I'm staying here").
"It was a horrible time for Fiorentina fans," Lorenzo Lepore, Fiorentina fan and owner of SV Media, told ESPN. "The club is part of daily life in Florence. It was very hard for Fiorentina fans to accept -- the club hadn't cheated, instead it was the owners who let us down." For Fiorentina, gone were the trips to AC Milan and Inter Milan as they rebuilt, instead they planned for car rides to Aglianese and Poggibonsi.
The scene that greeted players and management on their first days back in as Fiorentia Viola was grim. "I arrived on August 13, but there was nothing," then-manager Pietro Vierchowod said in a 2017 interview. "With sporting director Giovanni Galli, I went to a shop to get balls and shirts, and at the first training sessions I only had five Primavera players.

items.title: Ruto: Kenya saves Sh1.5bn as national exam papers are printed locally
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 18 – Kenya has printed national examination papers locally for the first time in 65 years, President William Ruto has announced, marking a major shift in the country’s examination administration.
Speaking during his fourth State of the Nation Address to Parliament, Ruto said the
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 18 – Kenya has printed national examination papers locally for the first time in 65 years, President William Ruto has announced, marking a major shift in the country’s examination administration.
Speaking during his fourth State of the Nation Address to Parliament, Ruto said the milestone had been achieved as the country administered national examinations to 3.6 million learners sitting the Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA), Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA) and Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE).
“For the first time in 65 years, examination papers were printed here in Kenya,” Ruto said.
The President said the examinations had been conducted in a calm and orderly atmosphere, without the anxiety, tension and intimidating security deployments that had characterised previous examination periods.
“The examinations have been conducted in a calm and orderly atmosphere, free from the anxiety, tension and intimidating security deployments of the past. This is how it should be,” he said.
He added that examinations should be treated as a normal part of the learning process rather than an intimidating exercise.
“Examinations are a normal part of learning, not a security operation or a matter of life and death. They should assess our children’s progress, not instil fear about their future,” Ruto said.
The announcement formed part of the President’s broader assessment of government investment in education, which he said was aimed at reducing the financial burden on households.
Ruto said his administration had recruited 100,000 teachers in four years and was preparing to employ an additional 20,000 to address the shortage of teachers in public schools.
“When we assumed office, Kenya faced a teacher shortage estimated at 116,000,” he said, adding that parents had previously been forced to contribute towards the employment of teachers through Boards of Management.
The President also said the government had constructed 23,000 classrooms and was constructing and equipping 1,600 laboratories to improve learning facilities.
He disclosed that annual government allocation to the education sector had risen from Sh521 billion in the 2022/23 financial year to Sh784 billion in the current financial year.
Ruto called on schools to ensure public resources reached learning institutions promptly and were managed responsibly, warning against imposing unauthorised charges on parents.
“Parents should not be required to carry public obligations through unauthorised charges,” he said.
He maintained that increased public investment in education was intended to make learning more affordable while equipping children with skills necessary for employment and economic productivity.

items.title: Sam Altman warns against a future where AI, not humans, calls the shots
items.summary: OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives. Speaking at The New York Times Dealbook Summit on Wednesday, the AI executive referred to discussions in Silicon Valley about wheth
items.text:
OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives. Speaking at The New York Times Dealbook Summit on Wednesday, the AI executive referred to discussions in Silicon Valley about whether there will be a gradual handover to AI—meaning AI will eventually become the decision-making authority across every major industry and institution.
“One thing we’ve been talking a lot about recently is there’s been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future, and there’s increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And I — we both — agree that that’s a terrible idea,” said Altman, who was sharing the stage with OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman.
The handoff theory stems from the idea that as AI models become increasingly more powerful, they will learn to improve themselves — a concept known as “recursive self-improvement” or RSI. As existing AI technology builds newer, smarter generations, those will eventually become a superintelligence that humans can no longer control, the belief goes.
Altman explained that he and Brockman only disagree over how to best accomplish the goal of keeping humans in control, or what sort of challenges we should expect to face along the way. However, Altman characterized this as more of a debate between two people who share the same larger views.
“The question of how to actually prevent [handover] from happening — how to actually ensure that we will, given all of the various pressures and given what other companies may try to do — that we are going to actually ensure that people stay in control of the future in a very deep way, and we don’t have this either accidental or intentional handover — I think we can both agree on that,” Altman said.
Brockman added that, as the models improve, there’s an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, and security, which may require changes in how things are currently done.
“Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new…technology,” he said.
Today, AI researchers monitor the model’s chain of thought, where the AI writes out what it’s thinking as it works through problems and performs tasks. But in Brockman’s view, that may not always be the best way to monitor more advanced AI that’s being built now.
“As the models have gotten more capable, they can do more within just the forward path without having to actually write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring,” Brockman said. “We’re going to need to deliver that, and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about, as the capabilities get to a certain point, chain-of-thought monitorability is degraded,” he continued, adding that all the problems were technical ones to be solved.
OpenAI had committed to increased chain-of-thought monitoring after the incident where an OpenAI model escaped containment and hacked into the AI model repository Hugging Face. In today’s interview, Brockman noted that the company told 25% of its production engineers to stop building things and work on securing the AI technology after the hack.
But despite the high-profile breach, he argued that forward progress was still critical to fight bad actors.
“I think to realize that if you look to the level of capabilities of models in the world, and you see cyber models that are coming from that are now…in the hands of threat actors everywhere, that I think that it’s really important that defenders use the most capable models to defend,” he said.

items.summary:
Rassie Erasmus: South Africa coach invites fans to watch-along of Springboks clash vs Ireland following six-match ban
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was handed a six-match suspension for comments he made about referees following South Africa's Nations Championship defeat by France; South Africa Rug
items.text:
Rassie Erasmus: South Africa coach invites fans to watch-along of Springboks clash vs Ireland following six-match ban
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was handed a six-match suspension for comments he made about referees following South Africa's Nations Championship defeat by France; South Africa Rugby have requested a full hearing into his ban
Wednesday 18 November 2026 17:44, UK
Rassie Erasmus has invited fans to join a live watch-along online of South Africa's clash against Ireland, after the Springboks coach was suspended for six matches for comments he made about match officials.
Erasmus had questioned whether there were double standards in the officiating of South Africa's 21-19 defeat to France during a press conference earlier in the week, prompting an investigation from World Rugby, who later said that the coach had "disrespected the authority of the officials".
He will now be unable to have any match-day involvement in his side's Nations Championship match against Ireland on Saturday, or their Nations Championship Finals match, commencing the following week.
South Africa have requested a full hearing in response to the sanction and on Wednesday, Erasmus broke his silence, inviting members of the public to join him to watch Saturday's game via a live stream.
"Can sit and moan or make the best of it," the Springboks coach wrote in a post on X.
"I'll be watching the match at the hotel. Not keen to watch [it] on my own.
"So, let's give it a go and hope I get the 'tech' sorted = TV on, My Laptop camera on, and you're welcome to join me.
"Sign up here (adults 18+): http://watchwithrassie.com. This is personal, not official."
On his streaming website, Erasmus has embedded a video of a flying South Africa flag, with a link to sign up to watch.
The 54-year-old, who guided South Africa to back-to-back Rugby World Cups in 2019 and 2023, provided some more details on the webpage about how the live stream would work.
"We each watch on our own TV, and I'll be on camera so you can see me watch it too. Send me a message and I'll read some out."
A disclaimer on the page read: "This is me personally, Rassie. It is not an official team or Springbok channel."
It is unclear when Erasmus will be able to return to coach South Africa, but he is expected to be available for the 2027 Rugby World Cup.
On Tuesday, World Rugby confirmed an independent panel had reviewed the comments made by Erasmus under World Rugby's Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, a framework that was introduced in July.
"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," the governing body said in a statement.
"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity."
Erasmus: Manipulation of the game or the result?
On Monday, Erasmus claimed France should have been given three yellow cards for illegal tackles as he leapt into a rant criticising referees.
"Let's say 11 of those were at least a penalty and three I thought were at least three yellow cards. And not one was sanctioned and not one was shown out or cited," Erasmus said.
"I'll send you the playlist, but I'll get into trouble… So I can't send the playlist to anybody and we can only send five clips to World Rugby. So we'll probably query it, but the answer will probably be: 'Yes, it was a mistake; it should have been penalised'.
"On numerous times we mentioned to the referee 'we think there's a knee-drop tackle'. I'm saying to you, my feeling is that knee-drop tackles is out. They happened 17 times in our game. Not one was penalised.
"And if the TMO didn't see it, then maybe technology must be better. If he saw it and ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result? Or players getting injured?
"So, all I'm asking is don't take the TMOs out and discourage them from getting involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."
World Rugby has since received backlash on social media in the wake of Erasmus' ban, and South Africa Rugby has condemned the abuse.
"SA Rugby unequivocally condemns any form of intimidation, threats or personal attacks. Such behaviour has no place in rugby and is entirely contrary to the values upon which our game is founded."

Carlos Alcaraz continued his perfect run at the ATP Finals with a win over Daniil Medvedev; the Spaniard called for his physio after appearing to pull up with a hamstring problem; watch the ATP Fin
items.text:
ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz defies injury concerns to continue flawless run with win vs Daniil Medvedev
Carlos Alcaraz continued his perfect run at the ATP Finals with a win over Daniil Medvedev; the Spaniard called for his physio after appearing to pull up with a hamstring problem; watch the ATP Finals live on Sky Sports
Wednesday 18 November 2026 18:22, UK
Carlos Alcaraz kept up his strong end-of-season form with a 6-2 6-4 victory over Daniil Medvedev at the ATP Finals on Wednesday despite taking a medical timeout and getting his left thigh strapped.
Seven-time Grand Slam champion Alcaraz extended his winning streak to 11 matches as he seeks a third consecutive indoor title after trophies in Vienna and Paris.
He will now qualify for the semi-finals of the elite eight-man event if Frances Tiafoe wins a set against Flavio Cobolli in the other group match later.
- Keep track of the full tennis schedule live on Sky Sports
- Download Sky Sports app for analysis, news and video 📺
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW📱
Alcaraz conceded only four games to Tiafoe in his opener.
World No 1 Medvedev moves to a record of 1-1 for the tournament after he beat Cobolli on Monday.
Alcaraz's win was his fifth in six matches against top-five players this year. His lone loss came against Jannik Sinner in the Monte Carlo Masters final.
Alcaraz 'feeling OK' despite medical timeout
After breaking Medvedev twice in the first set, Alcaraz was forced to call for treatment in the second set.
"I was playing great and suddenly I felt a little problem in my hamstring," Alcaraz said.
"But just a little bit. I mean, I could play really good tennis since that moment until the end of the match.
"I was trying to stay relaxed, to move not too aggressively.
"Right now I'm just feeling OK. We will see with my team, with my physio, but I think the rest of the day and tomorrow is really going to be important."
Alcaraz missed this year's French Open and Wimbledon after he was ruled out for four and a half months due to a right wrist injury.
Henman: Injury proves no distraction for Alcaraz
Sky Sports Tennis' Tim Henman said:
"I don't expect, even at this stage, he [Alcaraz] knows how serious this [injury] is.
"Whether he has been compensating, trying to protect his knee and now it's gone to his hamstring, his quad on the other leg.
"What could have been a distraction, just didn't really materialise, because his tennis is faultless.
"Where do you attack? He's so fast from the back of the court and is so good off both wings. He changes direction. You hit a great shot; he hits a slice back. He can stay in the rally and defend. His serving has been so consistent.
"We've seen him play like this on other surfaces; outdoors hard, on clay, on grass.
"But this level indoors is even new for him."

items.title: Zverev notified of lawsuit by ex-partner during ATP Finals
items.summary:
Alexander Zverev notified of lawsuit by former partner in abuse case during middle of ATP Finals
Alexander Zverev has been notfied about a lawsuit filed by his ex-partner during ATP Finals; world No 1 advanced to the semi-finals of the season-ending tournament on Tuesday night
Wednesday 18 November
items.text:
Alexander Zverev notified of lawsuit by former partner in abuse case during middle of ATP Finals
Alexander Zverev has been notfied about a lawsuit filed by his ex-partner during ATP Finals; world No 1 advanced to the semi-finals of the season-ending tournament on Tuesday night
Wednesday 18 November 2026 18:41, UK
World No 1 Alexander Zverev was officially notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals on Wednesday.
The latest legal case brought by the mother of Zverev's former partner alleges the tennis player violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her.
The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an interview with French sports news outlet L'Equipe earlier this year that "it has been proven that the accusations were false" and "my innocence has been proven."
Zverev's Berlin-based lawyers, Christian Schertz and Anna Sophie Heuchemer, confirmed in a statement shared with The Associated Press that they were formally served with Patea's lawsuit on Wednesday.
"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit," Zverev's lawyers said. "If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion" protected by the German constitution.
They said there had been no breach of any contractual obligations.
Patea's lawyer, Michael Scheele, told The Associated Press that Zverev's claim over his innocence "triggered a veritable storm of criticism against our client."
He said the backlash was damaging to her business as an influencer and that she also felt her honour had been violated.
"Quite apart from the fact that Zverev's claim is false, he was not permitted to make any public statements whatsoever, in any form," he said. "Both Brenda Patea and Alexander Zverev had agreed to this in a settlement."
Patea is seeking that Zverev be ordered not to repeat such comments and that he be fined up to £208,484 €250,000 euros every time if he does.
Zverev faced a charge of causing bodily harm to Patea during an argument in Berlin in May 2020. He always denied any wrongdoing.
The case ended in a district court in Berlin in 2024 after the settlement. Zverev agreed to pay fines to the state and charitable organisations.
Zverev this month ascended to the No 1 ranking for the first time. He also won his first two Grand Slam titles this year and is competing this week at the ATP Finals in Turin.
Zverev has not commented on the lawsuit.
He previously denied abuse allegations from another former girlfriend, Olga Sharypova, who first made the accusations in 2020 and followed up in 2021 with a detailed account in a Slate.com article that was taken down because of a preliminary injunction issued by a German court. Slate said it stood by the article.
The allegations prompted the men's professional tennis tour, the ATP, to investigate her claims. It ended 15 months later, in January 2023, with the ATP saying there was "insufficient evidence" to substantiate the claims.

items.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it’s ‘hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen’
items.summary: The AI industry is entering a new era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scand
items.text:
The AI industry is entering a new era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, raising potentially far-reaching national security concerns.
Speaking onstage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman each revealed that they had spoken privately with Huang as the embattled former CEO’s public image continued to unravel.
“Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”
OpenAI has worked closely with Huang over the years. Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips that power OpenAI’s technology.
Brockman added that he and his wife are friends with Huang’s family, so the couple had reached out “personally, just to be there for him and his family at this time.”
“I think it’s obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company,” Brockman said. “I think that… what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last, and so we’re excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.”
Huang’s impact on Nvidia and the broader AI industry has been so profound that nearly 200,000 people, including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate him. Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that they have does not plan to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.
Altman was reticent to weigh in on Huang’s future at Nvidia. When asked whether he thought Huang could return, Altman replied, “One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory.”
“I will say, I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best,” Altman said. “I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

items.title: The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry
items.summary:
The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry
- Published

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the
items.text:
The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry
- Published
Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.
But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.
Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.
Sunderland, sandwiching the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.
But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.
The bottom three may already be taking shape
Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.
In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.
For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.
Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.
That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.
Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.
It's not all bad news for the bottom three
This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.
They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.
The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.
This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.
Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.
Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.
Tight at the bottom - and in the middle
While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.
Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.
Sunderland's eight points is also the most the side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.
In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.
The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for United next season.
Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.
Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.
That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.
The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.
The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.
As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.
That season West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.
Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

items.title: Seven new models at scalable price-performance
items.summary:
MAI Licensed Weights: Frontier performance you control
At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability.
But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you ru
items.text:
MAI Licensed Weights: Frontier performance you control
At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability.
But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24-7 doing real engineering work.
That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance:
Here’s the lineup:
Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24-7. That’s why MAI Cyber 2 Flash was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost.
Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools.
MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price.
MAI Code 2 is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price.
We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.
MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot today. Read more here.
MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in GitHub Copilot and in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry.
MAI Image 2.7 is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And MAI Image 2.7 Flash brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry here.
MAI Realtime 1 is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in MAI Labs and register your interest here.
Dragon Copilot Transcribe, built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians.
Decision 1.1 provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the AA Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol.
We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model.
And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data?
We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 50x cheaper cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives.
Today, we’re taking a big step forward with MAI Licensed Weights: models under your control.
Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment.
You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents.
So that’s MAI, a family of world class models with exceptional price performance: the world’s best image editing model; the world’s best transcription model; frontier cyber defense at 2% of the cost; and world class everyday coding models at a price you can scale.
And crucially all of it with Your IQ. Your agents. Your weights. All under your control.
This is Frontier Intelligence you can trust, from the company you can trust.

items.title: USWNT squad: Emma Hayes names veteran group for Concacaf championship and World Cup qualifier
items.summary: In the two years since the Paris Olympics, Emma Hayes has thoroughly tested fresh faces and new combinations, gathering a considerable amount of data about the US women’s national team. It’s been a thorough process, with 33 players earning their first caps since Hayes assumed the post, to bring her
items.text:
In the two years since the Paris Olympics, Emma Hayes has thoroughly tested fresh faces and new combinations, gathering a considerable amount of data about the US women’s national team. It’s been a thorough process, with 33 players earning their first caps since Hayes assumed the post, to bring her roster of options to 61 players.
At last, the main event is nearing. On Black Friday, the United States will enter the Concacaf W Championship with a clear objective: beat El Salvador. Winning the whole thing is nice, of course, and the USWNT have done so in nine of its 11 installments to date. But by far the most important game on that journey is the first one, a 27 November quarter-final date with clear stakes: overcome El Salvador or rely on a playoff to reach next summer’s World Cup.
Hayes’s 23 selections for the tournament suggests what her preferred core may look like for the remainder of the cycle. Only four field players on her roster arrive with fewer than a dozen caps: midfielder Croix Bethune (seven), who sent the Kansas City Current to the NWSL championship last weekend with a brilliant curling free-kick, plus defenders Kennedy Wesley (nine), Kate Del Fava (one) and Evelyn Shores, who becomes only the second uncapped USWNT player selected for a World Cup qualifier (following Taylor Flint, née Kornieck, 2022).
Eight players from Hayes’s Olympic gold medal squad remain in the fold, including the star attacking trio of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Sophia Wilson. Sam Coffey returns after an injury prevented her from joining the team in the previous window, while Naomi Girma misses out due to persistent muscle issues. Claudia Dickey, Mandy McGlynn and Phallon Tullis-Joyce will continue to vie to start in goal, continuing their open competition following Alyssa Naeher’s retirement. The average age of this roster is 26.1, with only two players (Lindsey Heaps and Rose Lavelle) at least 30.
The Concacaf W Championship doubles as qualifying for both the 2027 Women’s World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. All four semi-finalists will be guaranteed a spot in the World Cup field, and the top three finishers will also join the Olympic field. (The US have qualified for the Olympics automatically as hosts). The losing teams in the quarter-finals will compete against each other for Concacaf’s two spots in the inter-confederation playoffs, which are scheduled for February in Morocco.
This story will be updated with remarks from Hayes’s presser on Wednesday morning.

items.text:
CME Group Tour Championship: Field, format, prize money as Nelly Korda, Charley Hull, Lottie Woad battle for win at LPGA finale
Key questions about the CME Group Tour Championship, as the LPGA Tour’s 2026 season-long points race comes to an end; watch all four rounds live on Sky Sports
Wednesday 18 November 2026 16:28, UK
Who will be crowned the LPGA Tour’s Race to the CME Globe Champion? Who can stop Nelly Korda from winning? Can Brits Charley Hull and Lottie Woad claim victory? We get you up to speed ahead of this week’s LPGA Tour 2026 season finale, live on Sky Sports.
What is the CME Group Tour Championship?
The CME Group Tour Championship is the final event in the LPGA Tour's season-long points race.
Throughout 2026, players have competed in the LPGA Tour's points competition, the Race to CME Globe.
- Latest LPGA Tour headlines and results
- Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
- What golf is live on Sky Sports and when? Full TV listings
The top 60 players on the Race to CME Globe Points List are invited to feature at this weekend's event and the player who wins the 2026 CME Group Tour Championship will be crowned the Race to CME Globe champion.
Where is the CME Group Tour Championship held?
The tournament is held at the Tiburon Golf Club at the Ritz-Carlton Golf Resort in Naples, Florida.
The course has hosted the tournament since 2013.
Who can beat Korda?
It is the second time in consecutive years that Korda has arrived at the CME Group Tour Championship sitting at the top of the Race to CME Globe standings.
The American has already been crowned the Rolex Player of the Year, with three events to spare, but has never won the Race to CME Group Tour Championship. A first title this week would see her qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame.
Standing in her way is a field of the LPGA Tour's best players, including two-time CME Group Tour Championship winner Jeeno Thitikul, who arrives in Florida having won four times on the LPGA Tour this season.
Miyu Yamashita, who has three wins on the LPGA Tour in 2026, enjoyed a strong finish to her season, winning twice while placing inside the top 10 three times in her last six events.
Haeran Ryu, who clinched back-to-back majors at The Amundi Evian Championship and the KPMG Women's PGA Championship, also comes into this event off the back of a fine vein of form, finishing tied-second and tied-third in her last two starts.
What Brits are playing?
Hull clinched the first LPGA Tour title of her career at this event back in 2016, so she certainly knows how to win at Tiburon Golf Club.
It's been a great year for Hull, who won the Solheim Cup with Team Europe in September and placed inside the top 10 at five LPGA Tour events. She'll no doubt want to end the season in style with a win.
Woad is the only other English player in the field. She too has enjoyed an excellent year, winning the Kroger Queen City Championship in May and finishing tied-ninth at last week's The ANNIKA, marking her seventh top-10 finish of the season.
What's the prize pot?
A total prize purse of £8.33m ($11m) is up for grabs, with the winner set to take home a £3.03m ($4m) cheque, the biggest cash prize in the history of women's golf.
The runner-up is also set to receive £757,423 ($1m).
What other end-of-season awards are up for grabs?
The LPGA Tour will also award the golfer with the lowest scoring average across the 2026 season with The Vare Trophy.
While Korda holds the lowest average score for the year, she has not played enough rounds to qualify for the award, meaning Yamashita, who has a scoring average of 69.50 and Thitikul, who follows her at 69.87, will battle it out to win The Vare Trophy.
How to watch the CME Group Tour Championship?
Sky Sports will be showing all four rounds of the CME Group Tour Championship live.
The first two rounds of the tournament will be shown live on Sky Sports Mix from 7pm on Thursday and Friday, with the action also live from 8pm on both days.
The third round coverage starts at 6pm on Saturday on both Sky Sports Mix and Sky Sports Golf, while Sunday's action is also live from 6pm on Sky Sports Golf and Sky Sports+.
Coverage of the final round will begin at 6pm on Sky Sports+.

items.title: AI agents ask better questions than KPMG accountants in audit trial
items.summary: LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than it
items.text:
LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team.
The experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an important development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how quickly will the economics of auditing change?
According to the Financial Times, the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions.
Join The European Business Briefing
New subscribers this quarter are entered into a draw to win a Rolex Submariner. Join 40,000+ founders, investors and executives who read EBM every day.
Subscribe
KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into issues than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised.
The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged.
From supporting accountants to conducting audits
Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow.
The agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation.
The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the company’s accounts.
Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks.
KPMG plans to expand the initiative to as many as 20 larger audits, although the firm acknowledges that the technology is not yet sufficiently mature to be deployed across thousands of engagements. Data quality also remains a significant obstacle, with some businesses lacking the clean, structured information required for AI agents to operate effectively.
A challenge to the Big Four business model?
The implications for the accountancy industry could be substantial.
Traditional auditing relies on large teams of junior accountants undertaking detailed and repetitive work, supervised by experienced managers and partners. AI agents potentially offer a different operating model, automating significant portions of data collection, analysis and documentation while allowing senior professionals to concentrate on complex judgements and exceptions.
For firms such as KPMG, Deloitte, PwC and EY, the attraction is clear: faster audits, potentially lower operating costs and the ability to analyse much larger volumes of financial information.
However, whether those savings will ultimately be passed on to clients remains uncertain. KPMG has acknowledged the potential for significant time savings but has not confirmed whether AI-driven efficiencies will translate into lower audit fees.
Human judgement remains the final safeguard
The transition also presents regulatory and professional challenges. The UK’s Financial Reporting Council has warned that the use of AI must not undermine auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism.
There are also concerns about data security, over-reliance on automated conclusions and the possibility of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. The fundamental responsibility for an audit opinion remains with the human auditor, regardless of the technology used.
The KPMG experiment does not establish that AI can replace accountants or independently deliver a reliable statutory audit. It does, however, demonstrate that AI agents are beginning to challenge professionals in areas that were once considered dependent on human expertise.
For the accountancy profession, the question is no longer simply whether AI will become part of the audit process. It is how much of that process will eventually be performed by machines — and what role human accountants will play when it does.

items.title: Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either
items.summary: This summer, OpenAI paused its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face and early evidence suggested that its next model could independently find and exploit security flaws. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing advances in the
items.text:
This summer, OpenAI paused its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face and early evidence suggested that its next model could independently find and exploit security flaws. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing advances in the most powerful AI models, warning that they could be used to launch cyberattacks or become harder for their own creators to control.
Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either
Nvidia and AMD earnings show booming demand. This is why a frontier slowdown might not derail it.
It was a strange moment for the AI boom. The people building the most powerful models were warning about what those models might be capable of, and investors were suddenly wondering what would happen to chip demand if the labs eased up on new models. US chip stocks bore the brunt of the sell-off.
“Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend.”
Despite the hubbub it created, whatever slowdown there was appears to have been short-lived. OpenAI had announced only a two-week pause; it restarted the run 10 days later, at the end of August, though it continued to “temporarily hold back some smaller experimental training runs.” Anthropic released upgraded versions of its Fable and Mythos frontier models in November, touting improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision.
And the companies selling the chips powering those advances are doing better than ever.
Nvidia on Tuesday posted a blockbuster quarter, with data center revenue rising 110 percent from a year ago to $107.6 billion in the three months ended October 25. The chip designer began shipping its most advanced AI computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” The Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments alone. The racks are already running at CoreWeave, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle. Meta plans to expand Vera Rubin deployments to train and run AI models and agents.
Nvidia name-dropped Anthropic and OpenAI, too. Anthropic has expanded access to Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers and continues to work with Nvidia on future chip designs tailored to its workloads. OpenAI is among the companies adopting Nvidia’s new Vera CPUs.
“Proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic continue to advance the frontier,” Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on the earnings call. She said the company expects major frontier labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its data center revenue this fiscal year. Nvidia also raised its revenue growth forecast for next fiscal year from 70 percent to 75 percent.
Chipmaker AMD, meanwhile, reported its biggest quarter ever earlier this month, with revenue up 45 percent to $13.4 billion. Data center sales drove that growth, nearly doubling to $8.5 billion. OpenAI and Anthropic were among the first customers running workloads on AMD’s new high-end Helios systems, which use its latest MI450 GPUs.
Broadcom, which helps many of the biggest AI companies design their own custom chips, has yet to report earnings. But so far, there’s little sign of a frontier slowdown hurting chip sales.
Of course, even if AI labs were to significantly scale back their training ambitions, it would take a while to show up in chipmakers’ earnings. Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, told The Verge in September that it would take about six months to see the financial effects of a slowdown, owing to existing computing and memory procurement agreements. The impact could show up sooner in orders placed with chip manufacturers like TSMC.
So far, there’s little evidence of that, either: TSMC’s latest sales figures also show continued strength.
But there’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have.
“While one might argue the need for top-end GPUs will reduce with this shift toward inferencing, these workloads will collectively require more compute infrastructure than training,” Shah said. “Overall, it means a net increase in demand for all types of accelerators.”
There’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have.
According to our analysis of the latest data from corporate spending platform Ramp, frontier model families accounted for about 60 percent of token usage among businesses using Ramp in early November — a record high and about three times their share at the start of the year. That includes OpenAI’s Astra and Sol models and Anthropic’s Opus and Fable models.
But even as businesses use more AI, their spending is only growing modestly.
“It’s not really a demand issue though,” Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, tells The Verge. “By all measures, companies are using more AI.”
Rather, competition among AI model providers is driving down token prices so rapidly that it’s calling OpenAI and Anthropic’s revenue projections into question, Kharazian says.
That could prove beneficial for the companies supplying computing power. On Nvidia’s earnings call, Kress said token prices had fallen nearly 60 percent since May, spurring more usage. Meanwhile, rental prices for Nvidia GPUs across generations have gone up.
Nvidia and AMD are positioning their most powerful chips for both training and inference, including the demanding workloads created by AI agents.
That doesn’t necessarily mean Nvidia will maintain its dominance. As AI companies get more serious about the economics of serving their models to millions of people, they’re increasingly turning to custom chips that can do so more cheaply than general-purpose GPUs. items.title: Ruto defends 750km Northern Kenya road project amid past ridicule
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 18 – President William Ruto has announced plans to construct a 750-kilometre road corridor linking Isiolo, Wajir and Mandera counties in a major infrastructure push targeting historically marginalised parts of Northern Kenya.
Dubbed the Northern Kenya Gateway Corridor, the projec
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 18 – President William Ruto has announced plans to construct a 750-kilometre road corridor linking Isiolo, Wajir and Mandera counties in a major infrastructure push targeting historically marginalised parts of Northern Kenya.
Dubbed the Northern Kenya Gateway Corridor, the project is expected to improve transport links, connect remote communities to markets and unlock trade and investment opportunities across the region.
In his fourth State of the Nation Address to Parliament on Wednesday, Ruto said the road was part of his administration’s efforts to address historical inequalities in infrastructure development and extend economic opportunities to underserved communities.
The proposed corridor will run from Isiolo through Modogashe, Samatar and Wajir before extending to Tarbaj, Kotulo, Kobo, El-Wak, Garre and Rhamu, eventually reaching Mandera.
The President said the project was intended to give residents of Northern Kenya access to the same development opportunities enjoyed by communities in other parts of the country.
He recalled that his initial announcement of the project had attracted widespread jokes and social media parodies, with Kenyans poking fun at the long list of towns along the proposed route.
“When I first spoke about this road and named all the towns it would pass through, Kenyans had a field day. The jokes and parodies were everywhere. I saw some of them myself, and I must admit, some were quite hilarious,” he told Parliament.
He, however, said the public reaction had overlooked the significance of the project to millions of residents who have endured decades of poor road connectivity.
Ruto said some communities along the proposed route had lived their entire lives without a tarmacked road, leaving residents struggling to access markets, healthcare facilities and other essential services.
“Some have lived their entire lives without a single tarmacked road reaching their communities. Their entire lives. What many of us take for granted has remained a distant hope for other citizens,” he said.
He described the project as an expression of his administration’s commitment to equitable development, arguing that geographical location should not determine a citizen’s access to public investment and economic opportunities.
Invoking the slogan Usawa ni Sawa, Ruto said residents of Mandera deserved the same development opportunities as those living in Nairobi and other established urban centres.
The corridor is expected to ease the movement of people, livestock and goods, potentially reducing transportation costs and improving access to markets for traders and livestock producers. Better connectivity could also improve access to schools, hospitals and other public services in the largely remote region.
The announcement formed part of a broader infrastructure programme through which the President said his administration was seeking to expand the country’s road network and revive projects that had stalled over the years.
Ruto told Parliament that approximately 7,000 kilometres of roads were currently under construction across the country.
He said the Government was targeting the tarmacking of 28,000 kilometres of roads and the dualling of 2,500 kilometres of highways over the next decade.
The President argued that improved road infrastructure would lower the cost of doing business, facilitate the transportation of agricultural and manufactured goods, create employment and attract private investment.
He said road construction would be complemented by investments in electricity and water infrastructure to support businesses, expand industries and improve livelihoods in underserved regions.
The Northern Kenya Gateway Corridor is among the major infrastructure commitments Ruto is positioning as part of his administration’s broader promise to redistribute development and bring historically neglected regions into the national economy.

items.summary:

items.text:
Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.
Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.
The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.
We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.
We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.
Responsible disclosure timeline
October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability.
November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review.
November 16, 2026: Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5.
November 17, 2026: F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release.
November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure.
Overview
Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.
NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.
Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas, the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution, to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure.
The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.
Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.
In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2.
NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.
The Vulnerabilities
Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. items.title: Poland says it thwarted false flag operation near border with Kaliningrad
items.summary:
Russia reportedly planned mass-casualty sabotage attack in Poland to be blamed on Ukraine
Russian intelligence services reportedly planned to carry out a sabotage operation on Polish territory near the border with Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast in late October or early November which they intended to b
items.text:
Russia reportedly planned mass-casualty sabotage attack in Poland to be blamed on Ukraine
Russian intelligence services reportedly planned to carry out a sabotage operation on Polish territory near the border with Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast in late October or early November which they intended to be blamed on Ukraine.
Source: Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita, as cited by European Pravda
Details: The newspaper cited senior sources with ties to Poland's military and security services who are familiar with an operation carried out over the past two weeks to foil the Russian plot.
Rzeczpospolita said Warsaw had been warned of the planned operation by partner intelligence services, and Polish intelligence analysts had also identified signs of the threat.
"We had information about the specific sites that were to be attacked. The Russian plan envisaged mass casualties," one of the newspaper's sources said.
Drawing parallels with the Gleiwitz incident, a German false-flag operation carried out on 31 August 1939, another source said: "It was supposed to be something similar to Gleiwitz. Of course, those who crossed the border would most likely have been shot, or evidence that they had come from Ukraine would have been found on them. The aim was to stop aid to Ukraine."
Polish intelligence services took action after Russian intelligence officers responsible for coordinating sabotage operations appeared on the Russian side of the border. Such operations are mainly planned and coordinated by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU.
Police forces in areas bordering Russia were reinforced by officers from other parts of Poland in late October for this reason. Border Guard posts also received reinforcements, and additional Internal Security Agency officers were deployed to the area. Special forces held exercises in the Warmian-Masurian region, where Poland's Territorial Defence Forces had also held exercises earlier.
"The aim was deterrence, but also to ensure the ability to take pre-emptive action," a source familiar with the details said.
Rzeczpospolita asked Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland's Minister-Coordinator of Special Services, whether the Russians had planned to carry out a terrorist attack in Poland at a location where large numbers of people might have been present.
"I don't know the answer to that question – you'd have to ask the Russians, and they don't usually admit to planning such actions. Even if we have such information, we don't share it," he replied.
Siemoniak added, however: "If we took certain measures, it was because we considered the threat to be real.
In my opinion, all the measures taken in this case were appropriate. The available evidence indicated that the threat had been assessed as real," the minister said.
Background:
- In early November, a special operations headquarters was established at Poland's National Police Headquarters for an operation being conducted in the Warmian-Masurian and Podlaskie voivodeships. Security forces were preparing for possible acts of sabotage on the border with Kaliningrad Oblast.
- On 3 November, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that "suspicious activity" had been detected overnight on the Polish-Russian border.

items.title: Football Daily | From Cincinnati to Manchester: Pochettino in a hurry to paint town red
items.summary:
PLANES, CLAIMS AND AUTOMOBILES
With his team mired in the relegation zone and a massive match at Liverpool this weekend, Mauricio Pochettino has been understandably busy since being appointed head coach of Manchester United. Unfortunately for Old Trafford regulars, the small print of his contract me
items.text:
PLANES, CLAIMS AND AUTOMOBILES
With his team mired in the relegation zone and a massive match at Liverpool this weekend, Mauricio Pochettino has been understandably busy since being appointed head coach of Manchester United. Unfortunately for Old Trafford regulars, the small print of his contract meant the Argentinian was tied up masterminding victory for USA USA USA in the second leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti when he ought to have been in Carrington moving red magnets around a tactics board in front of Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Harry Maguire.
The match in Cincinnati was ostensibly a dead rubber, given the hosts kicked off with a 6-0 lead. However, the conditions of Pochettino’s release clause dictated he had to remain in charge until finishing his post-match media duties at the TQL Stadium. Like an errant spouse having one last dinner with their put-upon partner while their lover waits outside the restaurant with the engine running, Pochettino was unable to make his excuses and leave until the bill was settled. It was no surprise that his new role came up during his exit interview. In a playful exchange with DaMarcus Beasley, who spent a season on loan at Manchester City during the (Ben) Thatcher era, something of a gauntlet was thrown down to the departing boss. “Manchester is blue, it will always be blue,” honked the former international, who may be unaware of his former club’s disgrace and potentially imminent relegation to the North West Counties League.
“No way, you will see,” chuckled Pochettino by way of response. “Give me time. Give me time and that is going to change, for sure.” While the future colour scheme of football in Manchester almost certainly lies more in the hands of the three-person independent panel who will decide City’s fate after finding them guilty of industrial scale financial shenanigans, Pochettino assured fans he and his staff will do their bit to ensure the city will be painted red. “We are excited because the new challenge is a big challenge,” he whooped. “But at the same time, it’s the adrenaline that you want to feel. We are going to have a different job, but we have the experience to deal with that. We know that it is not a situation that deserves to be at a club like Manchester United and for the fanbase. The fanbase is amazing.”
Considering they’ve been flirting with Pochettino for nine years, most United fans will be unconcerned by his eventual arrival being delayed by an extra couple of days but, with that game against Liverpool to prepare for, the 54-year-old wasted little time in hightailing it to the airport and boarding a private jet for his new home. Upon arrival, he is expected to oversee his first training session, an event Sky Sports News has melodramatically anticipated using a serene, high-budget cinematic aesthetic that captures our Argentinian hero gazing longingly into a Manchester sunset. It’s a majestic, blockbuster shot that has rightfully become the subject of no end of online mockery. Football Daily wonders if we’ll see a contrasting shot on Sunday, when the Sky cameras cut to Pochettino staring in wide-eyed horror as Liverpool spank yet another goal past his side’s hapless defence.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
Join Sarah Rendell at 8pm GMT for updates on Chelsea 2-0 PSG in Women’s Bigger Cup.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“It’s wicked, the stuff I’ve done … going to Milan fashion week, being taken to Paris with brands like Christian Louboutin is a level I never thought I would reach or be possible when I first started it. Some of the people I’ve met doing it … when I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West … just celebrities and people that I grew up listening to and I feel like without that it probably wouldn’t have happened” – Omar Sowunmi gets his chat on with Will Unwin about his dual life as a top, top model and no-nonsense centre-back with Bromley.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 Thanks for drawing my attention to the ‘Pierre Sage playbook for unfussed continental coaches’ (yesterday’s Football Daily). Any info about where to order a copy? I’m asking for a newly-employed friend in Manchester” – Mike Wilner.
 When I first skimmed over mention of BigShoe (yesterday’s Still Want More? – full email edition), I was shocked to think the likes of Clark’s, Kickers and Bull Boys (signed by him, Alan Hansen) had formed a global order à la Big Tech, Big Pharma and (possibly) Big Website. Thankfully, it’s a rather life-affirming organisation. Kudos to them and all involved” – Martin Clifford.
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Martin Clifford. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.
